In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by the study of animal sounds, as shown by the criticisms about some major problems in the findings), there is progression (e.g., the regression made by the study of animal sounds, for a better understanding of animal communication and survival). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of behaviors, regardless of whether this be done by way of evasive manoeuvres or by way of charming manoeuvres), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of behaviors by way of evasive manoeuvres by a flying moth vis-à-vis a bat in the violent battle for survival—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of behaviors by way of charming manoeuvres by a male whale to a female whale in the seductive battle for reproduction). And the reverse direction also holds true. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 144 Sound, Earthquakes, and Seismology Another way to evaluate the possibility and desirability of sound from the perspective of nature is about sound, earthquakes, and seismology. The word “seismology” refers to “the scientific study of earthquakes and the propagation of elastic waves through the Earth. The field also includes studies of earthquake effects, such as tsunamis as well as diverse seismic sources such as volcanic, tectonic, oceanic, atmospheric, and artificial processes (such as explosions). A related field that uses geology to infer information regarding past earthquakes is paleoseismology.” (WK 2010p) So, a good way to study sound and earthquakes is to understand the nature of the waves propagated through the Earth and its surface, namely, “seismic waves.” Seismic Waves The term “seismic waves” refers to “elastic waves that propagate in solid or fluid materials. Because seismic waves commonly propagate efficiently and interact with internal structure, they provide the highest resolution noninvasive methods for studying Earth's interior.” (WK 2010p) There are two kinds of seismic waves through solids, namely, (a) “P- waves” (or “primary waves”) and (b) “S-waves” (or “secondary waves”). (WK 2010p) The two kinds of seismic waves are also known as “body waves” through solids (as opposed to “interface waves” through solid-air, as explained below). And a third kind of waves is known as “surface waves” (also known as “interface waves”) along a solid-air interface, which have two kinds, namely, “Rayleigh and Love” waves; but “[i]nterface waves can be theoretically explained in terms of interacting P- and/or S-waves.” (WK 2010p) Let us consider these different kinds of waves more closely in what follows. (a) Body Waves and Surface Waves The first major type of seismic waves is “pressure waves” (or “primary waves,” also known simply as P-waves”), which “are longitudinal waves that travel at maximum velocity within solids and are therefore the first waves to appear on a seismogram.” (WK 2010p) By contrast, the second major type of seismic waves is “S-waves” (or “transverse waves,” “shear waves,” or simply known as “secondary waves” instead), which are “transverse waves that travel more slowly than Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 145 P-waves and thus appear later than P-waves on a seismogram. Particle motion is perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation. Shear waves do not exist in fluids with essentially no shear strength, such as air or water.” (WK 2010p) Both “P-waves” and “S-waves” are “body waves,” because they travel through solids under the Earth. And the third type of seismic waves is “[s]urface waves” (also known as “interface waves”) which “travel more slowly than P-waves and S- waves, but because they are guided by the surface of the Earth (and their energy is thus trapped near the Earth's surface) they can be much larger in amplitude than body waves, and can be the largest signals seen in earthquake seismograms. They are particularly strongly excited when the seismic source is close to the surface of the Earth, such as the case of a shallow earthquake or explosion.” (WK 2010p) (b) Seismic Waves and Earthquakes Seismic waves are important to understand the nature of earthquakes, and they do not behave in the same way. For instance, “[o]ne of the earliest important discoveries (suggested by Richard Dixon Oldham in 1906 and definitively shown by Harold Jeffreys in 1926) was that the outer core of the Earth is liquid.” (WK 2010p) This layer of liquid has implications for P-waves and S-waves. The reason is that “S-waves” which “shake side-to-side” need “rigid material so they do not pass through the outer core. Thus, the liquid core causes a 'shadow' on the side of the planet opposite of the earthquake where no direct S-waves are observed.” (WK 2010p) In addition, when “P-waves…pass through the core,” the subsequent “reduction in P-wave velocity of the outer core also causes a substantial delay for P waves penetrating the core from the (seismically faster velocity) mantle.” (WK 2010p) Yet, “[u]sing seismic tomography with earthquake waves, the interior of the Earth has been completely mapped to a resolution of several hundred kilometers. This process has enabled scientists to identify convection cells, mantle plumes and other large-scale features of the inner Earth.” (WK 2010p) Earthquake Prediction and Its Problems All these findings are useful for earthquake prediction, but there are also unresolved problems. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 146 (a) Earthquake Prediction Nowadays, “seismographs are instruments that sense and record the motion of the Earth. Networks of seismographs today continuously monitor the seismic environment of the planet, allowing for the monitoring and analysis of global earthquakes and tsunami warnings, as well as recording a variety of seismic signals arising from non-earthquake sources ranging from explosions (nuclear and chemical), to pressure variations on the ocean floor induced by ocean waves (the global microseism), to cryospheric events associated with large icebergs and glaciers.” (WK 2010p) In fact, “[o]ne of the first attempts at the scientific study of earthquakes followed the 1755 Lisbon earthquake. Other especially notable earthquakes that spurred major developments in the science of seismology include the 1857 Basilicata earthquake, 1906 San Francisco earthquake, the 1964 Alaska earthquake and the 2004 Sumatra-Andaman earthquake.” (WK 2010p) (b) Prediction Problems However, there are also problems with “earthquake prediction,” which refers, in a technical sense, to the “forecasting of a probable timing, location, magnitude and other important features of a forthcoming seismic event.” (WK 2010p) Consider, for illustration, a few problems below. Firstly, one major problem with earthquake prediction is that it is so difficult to offer timely warnings well in advance for preparation. In fact, “[m]ost seismologists do not believe that a system to provide timely warnings for individual earthquakes has yet been developed, and many believe that such a system would be unlikely to give significant warning of impending seismic events.” (WK 2010p) Secondly, another major problem with earthquake prediction is that there are emergent phenomena in nature which are not entirely predictable, as uncertainty has a role to play too, and this is something that I already went to great lengths to explain in The Future of Complexity (2007) and The Future of Post-Human Geology (2010), for instance. This problem remains, even though “[m]ore general forecasts, however, are routinely used to establish seismic hazard.” (WK 2010p) And thirdly, still another major problem with earthquake prediction is that they are not very precise. For instance, “various attempts have been made by seismologists and others to create effective systems for precise earthquake predictions, including the VAN method. Such methods have yet to be generally accepted in the seismology community,” because they are not very accurate. (WK 2010p) Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 147 From a Broader Perspective But these criticisms against earthquake prediction should not be misleadingly misconstrued to dismiss its usefulness but are to show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of sound (from the perspective of nature with sound, earthquakes, and seismology as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders would on both sides like us to believe. More fundamentally, the analysis of sound, earthquakes, and seismology can teach us something refreshing about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness-relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness- vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution- transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute tendency of “S-waves” which do not travel “in fluids with essentially no shear strength, such as air or water”), there is relativeness (e.g., what is true for “S-waves” which travel only in solids is not so for “interface waves” which travel through solid- air). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g., the predictable tendency of seismologists to engage in “[m]ore general forecasts” about “seismic hazard”), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task for seismologists to make forecasts about “seismic hazard” which are very accurate and very timely). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g., the explanation by seismologists that they understand the interior of the Earth better nowadays, because of “seismic tomography with earthquake waves,” which allowed them, for instance, “to identify convection cells, mantle plumes and other large-scale features of the inner Earth”), there is inexplicability (e.g., the lack of sufficient explanation by seismologists of why they are still unable to predict earthquakes very accurately and very timely, if they think that they understand the interior of the Earth so well—since, for the critics, there can still be a lot of things that the sesimologists do not quite understand). And the reverse direction also holds true. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 148 In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise identification by earthquake engineers of some forecasts which are to estimate “the probability of…a particular size affecting a particular location within a particular time span”), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in this identification, since “[s]uch methods have yet to be generally accepted in the seismology community,” as they are not very accurate). (WK 2010p) And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple analysis of earthquake prediction by earthquake engineers), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated analysis of earthquake prediction by the critics who question the assumptions and claims by earthquake engineers, as shown in the criticisms). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of the correlation between earthquake prediction and the understanding of the interior of the Earth), there is hiddenness (e.g., the hidden bias in this supposed correlation, because of the assumptions and claims which have been questioned by the critics, such that earthquake prediction is not what the proponents would like us to believe). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of S-waves in solids), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more emtpy, concentration of “S-waves” in liquids). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower speed of S-waves to travel through solids, when compared with P-waves), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively faster speed of P-waves to travel through solids, when compared with S-waves). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relatively more developed ability of S-waves to travel through solids), there is contraction (e.g., the relatively less developed ability of S- waves to travel through liquids). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of body waves and surface waves in seismology), there is praxis (e.g., the practical application of the knowledge of body waves and surface waves to the field of earthquake engineering for earthquake prediction). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g,. the conventional wisdom about the core of the Earth as solids), there Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 149 is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to this conventional wisdom when “Richard Dixon Oldham in 1906 and…Harold Jeffreys in 1926” discovered that “the outer core of the Earth is liquid”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans in the state of nature to sense earthquakes when they occurred), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human understanding of earthquakes by the invention of seismographs for earthquake prediction before they even occurred). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the existence of body waves and surface waves), there is asymmetry (e.g., body waves travel through solids—but surface waves travel through solid-air). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by earthquake engineers, as shown by the problems pointed out by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by earthquake engineers for general earthquake forecasts). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values, regardless of whether this be done by way of earthquake engineering or by way of shamanism), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of earthquake engineering for a more secular lifeworld—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of shamanism for a more sacred lifeworld). And the reverse direction also holds true. Sound and Society Sound, when examined from the perspective of society, reveals to us some powerful features in relation to its possibility and desirability, and this can be shown by way of two case studies, namely, (2.4.1) sound, underwater acoustics, and naval warfare, and (2.4.2) sound, small talk, and social skills—to be addressed in what follows, in that order. Sound, Underwater Acoustics, and �aval Warfare An excellent case study to understand sound from the perspective of society has to do with sound, underwater acoustics, and naval warfare. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 150 As a start, the word “underwater acoustics” (or “hydroacoustics”) refers to “the study of the propagation of sound in water and the interaction of the mechanical waves that constitute sound with the water and its boundaries. The water may be in the ocean, a lake or a tank.” (WK 2010q) Generally speaking, “frequencies associated with underwater acoustics are between 10 Hz and 1,000,000 Hz. The propagation of sound in the ocean at frequencies lower than 10 Hz is usually not possible without penetrating deep into the seabed, whereas frequencies above 1,000,000 Hz are rarely used because they are absorbed very quickly.” (WK 2010q) As a field of study, “underwater acoustics is closely related to a number of other fields of acoustic study, including sonar, transduction, acoustic signal processing, acoustical oceanography, bioacoustics, and physical acoustics.” (WK 2010q) Sound in Water Sound in water has some distinctive features. Consider, for illustration, a few of them below, as summarized in Table 2.3. (a) Sound Waves The first feature of sound in water is that its “sound wave propagating underwater consists of alternating compressions and rarefactions of the water. These compressions and rarefactions are detected by a receiver, such as the human ear or a hydrophone, as changes in pressure. These waves may be man-made or naturally generated.” (WK 2010q) (b) Sound Absorption The second feature of sound in water is that sound absorption (or attenuation) at low frequency is “weak,” while “additional contributions at lower frequency in seawater are associated with the ionic relaxation of boric acid (up to c. 10,000 Hz) and magnesium sulfate (c. 10,000 Hz- 500,000 Hz).” (WK 2010q; R. Francois 1982) On the other hand, “[t]he main cause of sound attenuation in fresh water, and at high frequency in sea water (above 100,000 Hz) is viscosity.” (WK 2010q) In addition, “[s]ound may be absorbed by losses at the fluid boundaries. Near the surface of the sea losses can occur in a bubble layer or in ice, while at the bottom sound can penetrate into the sediment and be absorbed.” (WK 2010q; R. Francois 1982) Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 151 (c) Sound Reflection/Scattering The third feature of sound in water is that sound can reflect and scatter, both (c.1) in boundary interactions and (c.2) at target. (c.1) In relation to boundary interactions, “the water surface and bottom are reflecting and scattering boundaries.” (WK 2010q) At the water surface—“the sea-air surface can be thought of as a perfect reflector. The impedance contrast is so great that little energy is able to cross this boundary….At high frequency (above about 1,000 Hz) or when the sea is rough, some of the incident sound is scattered.” (WK 2010q) Another contribution is “the presence of wind generated bubbles or fish close to the sea surface. The bubbles can also form plumes that absorb some of the incident and scattered sound, and scatter some of the sound themselves.” (WK 2010q; D. Weston 1989; G. Norton 2001) And on the seabed—“[t]he acoustic impedance mismatch between water and the bottom is generally much less than at the surface and is more complex. It depends on the bottom material types and depth of the layers. Theories have been developed for predicting the sound propagation in the bottom” by N. Chotiros (1995) and M. Buckingham (2000). (WK 2010q) (c.2) In relation to target, “[t]he reflection of sound at a target whose dimensions are large compared with the acoustic wavelength depends on its size and shape as well as the impedance of the target relative to that of water. Formulae have been developed for the target strength of various simple shapes as a function of angle of sound incidence. More complex shapes may be approximated by combining these simple ones.” (WK 2010q; R. Urick 1983) (d) Sound Propagation The fourth feature of sound in water is that “[u]nderwater acoustic propagation depends on many factors,” like speed, depth, temperature, range, etc. (WK 2010q) In relation to speed—“[t]he direction of sound propagation is determined by the sound speed gradients in the water. In the sea the vertical gradients are generally much larger than the horizontal ones.” (WK 2010q) In relation to temperature—“[a]t equatorial and temperate latitudes in the ocean the surface temperature is high enough to reverse the pressure effect, such that a sound speed minimum occurs at depth of a few hundred metres. The presence of this minimum creates a special channel known as Deep Sound Channel, previously known as the SOFAR (sound fixing and ranging) channel, permitting guided propagation of underwater sound for The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 152 thousands of kilometres without interaction with the sea surface or the seabed.” (WK 2010q) And in relation to range—“as sound propagates underwater there is a reduction in the sound intensity over increasing ranges, though in some circumstances a gain can be obtained due to focussing. Propagation loss (sometimes referred to as transmission loss) is a quantitative measure of the reduction in sound intensity between two points, normally the sound source and a distant receiver….At short range the propagation loss is dominated by spreading while at long range it is dominated by absorption and/or scattering losses.” (WK 2010q) Sound for �aval Warfare The understanding of the main features of sound in water is not an idle exercise, since it has been used by the military in different countries for naval warfare, with the use of submarines as an excellent case in point. (WK 2010r) As countries increasingly use submarines for their navies, “submarine navigation undercover” needs to make good use of undercover acoustics, and “[t]he challenges of underwater navigation have become more important as submarines spend more time underwater, travelling greater distances and at higher speed.” (WK 2010r) After all, “[m]ilitary submarines travel underwater in an environment of total darkness with neither windows nor lights. Operating in stealth mode, they cannot use their active sonar systems to ping ahead for underwater hazards such as undersea mountains, drilling rigs or other submarines. Surfacing to obtain navigational fixes is precluded by pervasive anti-submarine warfare detection systems such as radar and satellite surveillance. Antenna masts and antenna-equipped periscopes can be raised to obtain navigational signals but in areas of heavy surveillance, only for a few seconds or minutes; current radar technology can detect even a slender periscope while submarine shadows may be plainly visible from the air.” (WK 2010r; A. Bivens 2004) Submarine navigation can be classified into two types for consideration, namely, (a) “surface and near-surface navigation, and (b) “deep water navigation,” as shown below and summarized in Table 2.3): (WK 2010r) (a) Surface and Near-Surface Navigation The surface and near-surface navigtion refers to “the surface” or the “periscope depth,” where submarines travel, with the use of the following methods to find out their position: (WK 2010r) Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 153 • “Satellite navigation” –“Global positioning system (GPS)—by entering waypoints internally, able to navigate at a more precise level.” –“NAVSAT” • “Terrestrial radio-based navigation systems; largely superseded by satellite systems” –“LORAN—seldom if rarely used anymore.” –“CHAYKA, the Russian counterpart of LORAN” –“OMEGA, the Western counterpart of the Alpha Navigation System, no longer in use” –“Alpha, the Russian counterpart of the Omega Navigation System” • “Celestial navigation using the periscope, or sextant—seldom used anymore due to advancement in technology” • “Radar navigation”—“radar signals are easily detected so radar is normally only used in friendly waters entering and exiting ports. With the implementation a more advanced radar system, many new techniques have been implemented in this process.” • “Active sonar”—“like radar, active sonar systems are readily detected, so active sonar is usually used only entering and exiting ports.” • “Pilotage”—“in coastal and internal waters, surfaced submarines rely on the standard system of navigational aids (buoys, navigational markers, lighthouses, etc.), utilizing the periscopes for obtaining lines of position to plot a triangulation fix.” • “Voyage Management System”—“referred to as the VMS, utilizes digital charts with other external sources fed in, to establish the ship's position. Other information may also be entered in manually in establishing a high quality fix or position.” Of course, there can be other methods, but these ones as cited above are the most important. (b) Deep Water Navigation By contrast, deep water navigation refers to “below periscope depth,” where “submarines determine their position” by using the following methods: (WK 2010r; UK 2010; JCS 2003; S. Hamn 1995) • “Dead reckoning course information obtained from the ship's gyrocompass” provides “measured speed and estimates of local ocean currents,” so “this could also be considered an estimated position as long as the ocean current is computed in.” The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 154 • “Inertial navigation system” is “an estimated position source, utilizes acceleration, deceleration, and pitch and roll in computing.” • “Bottom contour navigation may be used in areas where detailed hydrographic data has been charted and there is adequate variation in sea floor topography. Fathometer depth measurements are compared to charted depth patterns.” Again, there can be other methods, but these ones here are the most important. Problems with Submarine �avigation But submarine navigation is not without its own problems. Consider, for illustration, a few of them below, as summarized in Table 2.3. Firstly, one major problem with submarine navigation is that it does not always work, because submarines collide underwater from time to time with other submarines, drilling rigs, undersea mountains, and so on. For instance, even tthe USS San Francisco (SSN-711), known for its quietness underwater, “suffered substantial damage after colliding at high- speed with an undersea mountain” in 2005. (WK 2010r) Secondly, another major problem with submarine navigation is that submarines also become the target of “anti-submarine warfare detection systems such as radar and satellite surveillance.” (WK 2010r) And thirdly, still another major problem with submarine navigation is that submarines can be sunk by anti-submarine weapons and can also suffer substantial damage from internal explosion or from fire onboard sometimes. Favoring �o One But these criticisms against submarine navigation do not mean to totally reject its effectiveness for naval warfare but are to show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of sound (from the perspective of society with sound, underwater acoustics, and naval warfare as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. Moreover, the analysis of sound, underwater acoustics, and naval warfare reveals something important about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness- relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 155 principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the change-constancy principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution-transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness-hardness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute tendency of submarines to not use active sonar systems and radar navigation when in non-friendly waters), there is relativeness (e.g., what is true in non-friendly waters when submarines do not use active sonar systems and radar navigation in order to avoid detection is not necessarily so in friendly waters when submarines can use active sonar systems and radar navigation to enter and exit ports). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g., the predictable tendency of submarines to operate in stealth mode when in non-friendly waters, in order to avoid detection), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task to predict exactly which particular trip that a submarine takes in non-friendly waters will necessarily be successful, since it can collide underwater from time to time with other submarines, drilling rigs, undersea mountains, and so on). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g., the explanation that sound reflection/scattering on the seabed “depends on the bottom material types and depth of the layers,” as proposed by the theories developed by N. Chotiros and M. Buckingham, for instance), there is inexplicability (e.g., the lack of sufficient explanation in the theories of why there are not other important factors in determining sound reflection/scattering on the seabed, except material types and depth of the layers). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise identification of the seven important methods used by submarines for surface and near-surface navgiation), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the identification of the seven important methods, since it is not clear why there are seven of them, not nine, ten, and so on—or which one is the best overall, etc.). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple formulae which “have been developed for the target strength of various simple shapes as a function of angle of sound incidence”), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 156 more complex formulae for more complex shapes which “may be approximated by combining these simple ones”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open operation by submarines in friendly waters, by using active sonar systems and radar navigation, which can be easily detected), there is hiddenness (e.g., the stealth mode in which submarines travel when in non-friendly waters, in order to avoid detection). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of submarines using active sonar systems and radar navigation in friendly waters), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more empty, concentration of submarines using active sonar systems and radar navigation in non-friendly waters). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the change-constancy principle, if there is change (e.g., the ever new methods used by submarines for navigation over time), there is change (e.g., the ever constancy of the availability of methods to be used by submarines for navigation). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower speed of old submarines in the early days when traveling in deep water), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively quicker speed of new submarines nowadays when traveling in deep water). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relative expansion of the influence of “global positioning system” or GPS for submarine navigation nowadays), there is contraction (e.g., the relative contraction or decline of the influence of “terrestrial radio-based navigation systems” for submarine navigation nowadays). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of global positioning system or GPS), there is praxis (e.g., the practical application of GPS to submarine navigation for naval warfare). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional wisdom for ships in coastal and internal waters to rely on “the standard system of navigational aids…[like] buoys, navigational markers, lighthouses, etc.”), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to this standard system by the new way of satellite navigation). And the reverse direction also holds true. Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 157 In relation to the the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to live on land, unlike fish living in water), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human ability to live in water by the invention of submarines). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the co-existence of different navigation systems, like OMEGA and Alpha), there is asymmetry (e.g., the preferred usage of OMEGA in the West—but the preferred usage of Alpha in Russia). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., the use of GPS for civilian communication), there is hardness (e.g., the use of GPS for navel warfare). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by submarine navigation, as shown in the problems pointed out by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by submarine navigation for naval warfare). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors, regardless of whether this be done by way of stealthy submarine navigation or by way of open commercial ship navigation), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of stealthy submarine navigation for a more secretive lifeworld—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of open commercial ship navigation for a more transparent lifeworld). And the reverse direction also holds true. Sound, Small Talk, and Social Skills Another way to evaluate the possibility and desirability of sound from the perspective of society has to do with sound, small talk, and social skills. The term “small talk” here refers to a way to break the “awkward silence” by making some conversational noise about trivia (which is not to mean much of anything), that is, a kind of “conversation for its own sake” (or “comments on what is perfectly obvious.”), in that “[i]t is an informal type of discourse that does not cover any functional topics of conversation or any transactions that need to be addressed.” (WK 2010s & 2010t; B. Malinowski 1923) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 158 Th discourse on small talk “was initially studied in 1923 by Bronisław Malinowski, who coined the term phatic communion to describe it. The ability to conduct small talk is a social skill.” (WK 2010s) Social Functions of Small Talk Small talk, as a way to break “the awkward silence” in making some conversational noise so understood, serves some social functions, as summarized in Table 2.4. (WK 2010t) In other words, “small talk is a bonding ritual and a strategy for managing interpersonal distance. It serves many functions in helping to define the relationships between friends, work colleagues, and new acquaintances.” (WK 2010s; T. Bickmore 1999) Hereafter are three major examples of the social functions of small talk: (WK 2010s) • “In particular, it helps new acquaintances to explore and categorize each other's social position.” (J. Laver 1975) • “Small talk is closely related to the need for people to maintain positive face—to feel approved-of by those who are listening to them.” • “It lubricates social interactions in a very flexible way, although the desired function is often dependent on the point in the conversation at which the small talk occurs.” (J. Holmes 2000) There are three different points in a conversation at which small talk occurs, as shown below. (WK 2010s) • “At the Beginning of a Conversation”—this is “[w]here there is already a relationship between the two talkers, their small talk serves as a gentle introduction before engaging in more functional topics of conversation. It allows them to signal their own mood and to sense the mood of the other person. In a business meeting, it enables people to establish each other's reputation and level of expertise. When the talkers do not know each other, it allows them to show that they have friendly intentions and desire some sort of positive interaction.” • “At the End of a Conversation”—this is where “[s]uddenly ending an exchange may risk appearing to reject the other person. Small talk can be used to mitigate that rejection, affirm the relationship between the two people, and soften the parting.” • “As a Space Filler”—this is where “[in] many cultures, silences between two people are usually considered uncomfortable. Tension Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 159 can be reduced by starting phatic talk until a more substantial subject arises.” Surely, there are exceptions, and a good example concerns “couples in an intimate relationship,” which “can signal their level of closeness by a lack of small talk. They can comfortably accept silence in circumstances that would be uncomfortable for two people who were only casual friends.” (WK 2010s; A. Jaworski 2000) Topics of Small Talk Besides certain social functions, small talk has certain topics, which “usually depend…on any pre-existing relationship between the two people, and the circumstances of the conversation. In either case, someone initiating small talk will tend to choose a topic for which they can assume a shared background knowledge, to prevent the conversation being too one-sided.” (WK 2010s; J. Holmes 2000a) There are two kinds of topics here, namely, “either direct or indirect. Direct topics include personal observations such as health or looks. Indirect topics refer to a situational context such as the latest news, or the conditions of the communicative situation.” (WK 2010s; E. Ventola 1979) In any event, hereafter are four “safe” topics under “most circumstances”: (WK 2010s; J. Holmes 2000) • Ex: “The weather” • Ex: “Recent shared experiences, for example 'Good party last night, wasn't it?'” • Ex: “Television and films” • Ex: “Sports” However, there is a caveat here, in that “[t]he level of detail offered should not overstep the bounds of interpersonal space. When asked, 'How are you?' by an acquaintance they do not know well, a person is likely to choose a simple, generalised reply such as, 'Fine, thank you.' In this circumstance it would probably not be appropriate for them to reply with a list of symptoms of any medical conditions they were suffering from. To do so would assume a greater degree of familiarity between the two people than is actually the case, and this may create an uncomfortable situation.” (WK 2010s; J. Holmes 2000a) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 160 Patterns of Small Talk In addition, small talk follows some recognizable patterns. For instance, “Klaus Schneider [1988]…theorises that such a conversation consists of a number of fairly predictable segments, or 'moves,'” as shown below: (WK 2010s) • “The First Move”—“is usually phrased so that it is easy for the other person to agree. It may be either a question, or a statement of opinion with a tag question. For example, an opening line such as 'Lovely weather, isn't it?' is a clear invitation for agreement. • “The Second Move”—“is the other person's response. In functional conversations that address a particular topic, [H.] Grice's Maxim of Quantity [1975] suggests that responses should contain no more information than was explicitly asked for. Schneider claims that one of the principles of small talk contradicts the Maxim of Quantity. He suggests that politeness in small talk is maximised by responding with a more substantial answer. Going back to the example of 'Lovely weather, isn't it?', to respond by just saying 'Yes' is less polite than saying, 'Yes, very mild for the time of year.'” • “Subsequent Moves”—“Schneider describes that subsequent moves may involve an acknowledgement such as 'I see,' a positive evaluation such as 'That's nice,' or what's called 'idling behaviour,' such as 'Mmm,' or 'Really?'.” However, even here, there is certain social structure governing small talk, as explained below. Social Structure of Small Talk The social structure of small talk can be illustrated by way of its gender differences. For instance, “speech patterns between women tend to be more collaborative than those of men, and tend to support each other's involvement in the conversation. Topics for small talk are more likely to include compliments about some aspect of personal appearance. For example, 'That dress really suits you.' Small talk between women who are friends may also involve a greater degree of self disclosure. Topics may cover more personal aspects of their life, their troubles, and their secrets. This self-disclosure both generates a closer relationship between them, and also is a signal of that closeness.” (WK 2010s; D. Tannen 1992) Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 161 On the other hand, “men's small talk tends to be more competitive. It may feature verbal sparring matches, playful insults, and putdowns. However, in a way these are also both creators and signals of solidarity; the men are signalling that they are comfortable enough with each other's company to be able to say these things without their being taken as insults.” (WK 2010s) Problems with the Discourse on Small Talk But there are problems with this discourse on small talk. Consider, for illustration, some criticisms below, as summarized in Table 2.4. Firstly, one major criticism of the discourse on small talk is that, as Robert Merton (1968) once pointed out in his critique of functionalism in sociology, social functons can be “undesirable,” relative to different moral evaluations. (P. Baofu 2004: 69) In the case of small talk, it can degenerate into a waste of time for much gossiping about nothing. Secondly, another major criticism of the discourse on small talk is that, as Robert Merton (1968) also pointed out in his critique of functionalism in sociology, social functons “are not necessarily indispensable (since there can be 'functional alternatives,' 'functional equivalents or substitutes').” (P. Baofu 2004: 69) In the case of small talk, there can be alternative social functions not listed above. Thirdly, still another major criticism of the discourse on small talk is that, as Robert Merton (1968) also pointed out in his critique of functionalism in sociology, social functons do not necessarily exist, because “there exist 'nonfunctions' which are consequences…left over from previous historical epochs but no longer relevant to a current system. (G. Ritzer 2003:93-4)” (P. Baofu 2004: 69) In the case of small talk, it may well be much ado about nothing, especially when it ends up wasting much time in some cases. And fourthly, one more major criticism of the discourse on small talk is that whether it is appropriate or not to engage in small talk about a certain topic can be culturally relative. For instance, “[w]eather is a common topic in regions where the climate has great variation and can be unpredictable. Questions about the family are usual in some Asian and Arabic countries, although male followers of the Islamic faith avoid asking about another man's wife. In cultures that are highly status-oriented such as China and Japan, small talk between new acquaintances may feature numerous questions that enable social categorization of each other. In many European cultures it is The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 162 common to discuss the weather, politics or the economy, although in some countries personal finance issues such as salary are considered taboo.” (WK 2010s; G. Hofstede 2000; J. Grzega 2008) In Retrospect But these criticisms against the discourse on small talk do not mean to dismiss its validity outright but are to show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of sound (from the perspective of society with sound, small talk, and social skills as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. Moreover, the analysis of sound, small talk, and social skills can teach us something insightful about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness-relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability- inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the change-constancy principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution-transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness-hardness principle, the seriousness-playfulness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute norms of “male followers of the Islamic faith [to] avoid asking about another man's wife” in small talk), there is relativeness (e.g., what is not appropriate for “male followers of the Islamic faith [to]…ask…about another man's wife” in small talk” is not necessarily so for members of other societies, say, in the U.S., who may not mind). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g., the predictable tendency of small talk to address “[w]eather…in regions where the climate has great variation and can be unpredictable”), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task to predict exactly what particular aspects of weather a small talk at a given point will concern with). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g., the explanation that small talk is not needed in situations involving “couples in an intimate relationship,” which “can signal their level of closeness by a lack of small talk”), there is inexplicability (e.g., the lack of sufficient explanation, within this view, of Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 163 why the absence of small talk among couples in an intimate relationship cannot mean something else instead, like a relationship in crisis, and so on—not that this must necessarily imply good intimate relatinship). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise identification of four major “safe” topics under “most circumstances”), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the identification, since it is not clear why there must be these four major “safe” topics, not others, whether more or less). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple analysis of small talk in terms of its social functions), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated analysis of small talk by questioning its assumptions and claims, as shown in the criticisms). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of the relationship between small talk and social skills), there is hiddenness (e.g., the hidden bias in the discourse on small talk and social skills, because it dogmatically assumes that small talk is necessarily functional for better social skills). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of people who engage in small talk if they are not in an intimate relationship), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more empty, concentration of people who engage in small talk if they are in an intimate relationship). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the change-constancy principle, if there is change (e.g., the ever new topics of small talk over time), there is constancy (e.g., the ever constant existence of topics of small talk). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower speed of someone like H. Grice to give more info than was explicitly asked for in a small talk), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively quicker speed of someone like Schneider to give more info than was explicitly asked, because “politeness in small talk is maximised by responding with a more substantial answer”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relatively more developed ability of those who indulge in small The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 164 talk over time to improve their social skills), there is contraction (e.g., the relatively less developed ability of those who indulge in small talk over time to focus on serious conversation). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional wisdom about Grice's Maxim of Quantity, which suggests that responses should contain no more info than was explicitly asked for in small talk), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to this conventional wisdom about the Maxim of Quantity, by Schneider for a new view which suggested instead that it is polite to give more info than was explicitly asked for). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to engage in small talk over time in the state of nature), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human tendency to engage in small talk by the invention of some etiquettes like Grice's Maxim of Quantity and Schneider’s counter-proposal). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the co-existence of different etiquettes about small talk), there is asymmetry (e.g., Grice's Maxim of Quantity in the 1970’s—but Schneider’s counter-proposal in the 1980’s). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., the use of “compliments about some aspect of personal appearance” among women in small talk), there is hardness (e.g., the use of “verbal sparring matches, playful insults, and putdowns” among men in small talk). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the seriousness-playfulness principle, if there is seriousness (e.g.,the serious business of social functions in small talk), there is playfulness (e.g.,the playful nature of small talk, when men engage in “playful insults”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by small talk, as shown in the criticisms by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by small talk for the enhancement of social skills). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors, regardless of whether this be done by way of small talk or substantial talk), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 165 the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of small talk for a relatively smoother social world—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of substantial talk for a relatively blunter social world). And the reverse direction also holds true. Sound and Culture Sound, when examined from the perspective of culture, can cast an illuminating light on its possibility and desirability, and this can be shown by way of two case studies, namely, (2.5.1) sound, harmonic series, and musical culture, and (2.5.2) sound, and noise aesthetics—to be addressed in what follows, respectively. Sound, Harmonic Series, and Musical Culture An excellent case study here to understand sound from the perspective of culture has to do with sound, harmonic series, and musical culture. In Western culture, “musical acoustics or music acoustics is the branch of acoustics concerned with researching and describing the physics of music—how sounds employed as music work.” (WK 2010u) The Sound of Music To understand how sounds are employed as music work, it is important to be familiar with some important aspects of the sound of music, namely, (a) the physical aspect, (b) the psychological aspect, and (c) the musical aspect, as summarized in Table 2.5. (a) The Physical Aspect The first important aspect of the sound of music is physical, in relation to the physics of sound. To start, “[w]henever two different pitches are played at the same time, their sound waves interact with each other—the highs and lows in the air pressure reinforce each other to produce a different sound wave. As a result, any given sound wave which is more complicated than a sine [basic] wave can be modelled by many different sine waves of the appropriate frequencies and amplitudes (a frequency spectrum).” (WK 2010u) In the context of music, “[w]hen the original sound sources are perfectly periodic, the note consists of several related sine waves (which mathematically add to each other) called the fundamental and the harmonics, partials, or overtones.” (WK 2010u) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 166 To clarify these words (like “fundamental,” “overtones,” “partials,” and “harmonics”) further—it is important to remember that “[t]he fundamental is the frequency at which the entire wave vibrates. Overtones are other sinusoidal components present at frequencies above the fundamental. All of the frequency components that make up the total waveform, including the fundamental and the overtones, are called partials. Together they form the harmonic series.” (WK 2010u) (a) The Psychological Aspect The second important aspect of the sound of music is psychological, in relation to the psychology of sound. As a reminder, what is perceived as “sound” has to do with “[v]ariations in air pressure against the ear drum, and the subsequent physical and neurological processing and interpretation,” which then “give rise to the subjective experience called sound.” (WK 2010u) So, the subjective experience of the sound of music has to do with “periodic or regular vibrations rather than non-periodic ones” in the sound perceived, because “musical sounds typically have a definite pitch.” (WK 2010u) Then, “[t]he transmission of these variations through air is via a sound wave. In a very simple case, the sound of a sine wave, which is considered to be the most basic model of a sound waveform, causes the air pressure to increase and decrease in a regular fashion, and is heard as a very pure tone. Pure tones can be produced by tuning forks or whistling. The rate at which the air pressure oscillates is the frequency of the tone, which is measured in oscillations per second, called hertz. Frequency is the primary determinant of the perceived pitch. Frequency of musical instruments can change with altitude due to changes in air pressure.” (WK 2010u) (c) The Musical Aspect The third important aspect of the sound of music is musical, in relation to musical acoustics. Recall what is described above about the differences among different terms like “fundamental,” “overtones,” “partials,” and “harmonics”— which are important to understand the sound of music, like the nature of harmonic series. For instance, “[o]vertones which are perfect integer multiples of the fundamental are called harmonics. When an overtone is near to being harmonic, but not exact, it is sometimes called a harmonic partial, although they are often referred to simply as harmonics. Sometimes overtones are created that are not anywhere near a harmonic, and are just called partials or inharmonic overtones.” (WK 2010u) Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 167 There are different harmonics of course, because “[t]he fundamental frequency is considered the first harmonic and the first partial. The numbering of the partials and harmonics is then usually the same; the second partial is the second harmonic, etc.” (WK 2010u) However, “if there are inharmonic partials, the numbering no longer coincides. Overtones are numbered as they appear above the fundamental. So strictly speaking, the first overtone is the second partial (and usually the second harmonic). As this can result in confusion, only harmonics are usually referred to by their numbers, and overtones and partials are described by their relationships to those harmonics.” (WK 2010u) This caveat aside—“[if] two notes are simultaneously played, with frequency ratios that are simple fractions (e.g. 2/1, 3/2 or 5/4), then the composite wave will still be periodic with a short period, and the combination will sound consonant.” (WK 2010u) A good example is “a note vibrating at 200 Hz and a note vibrating at 300 Hz (a perfect fifth, or 3/2 ratio, above 200 Hz) will add together to make a wave that repeats at 100 Hz: every 1/100 of a second, the 300 Hz wave will repeat thrice and the 200 Hz wave will repeat twice. Note that the total wave repeats at 100 Hz, but there is not actually a 100 Hz sinusoidal component present.” (WK 2010u) Moreover, “the two notes will have many of the same partials. For instance, a note with a fundamental frequency of 200 Hz will have harmonics at”: (WK 2010u) (200,) 400, 600, 800, 1000, 1200,… And “a note with fundamental frequency of 300 Hz will have harmonics at”: (WK 2010u) (300,) 600, 900, 1200, 1500,… So, these “two notes have the harmonics 600 and 1200 in common, and more will coincide further up the series.” (WK 2010u) What is perceived as “harmony” in music is precisely this “combination of composite waves with short fundamental frequencies and shared or closely related partials.” (WK 2010u) Conversely, “[w]hen two frequencies are near to a simple fraction, but not exact, the composite wave cycles slowly enough to hear the cancellation of the waves as a steady pulsing instead of a tone. This is called beating, and is considered to be unpleasant, or dissonant.” (WK 2010u) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 168 Problems with the Sound of Music However, there are problems with this mainstream analysis of the sound of music. Consider, for illustration, some criticisms below, as summarized in Table 2.5. Firstly, one major criticism of this mainstream analysis of the sound of music is that what is perceived as “harmonic” also depends on “hearing sensitivity.” (WK 2010q; W. Richardson 1995) For instance, it is known that there are “differences in hearing sensitivity,” be they among humans or animals. And secondly, another major criticism of this mainstream analysis of the sound of music is that whether or not harmonic music is beautiful or not also depends on differences in cultural tradition. For instance, the American experimental composer John Cage is known for his fun with chaotic music—which is drastically different from harmonic music as portrayed above. Cage even made use of chance by using I Ching (and sometimes dice and coin too) in his musical composition. (O.Hardison 1989:171; P. Baofu 2000) Some like it, but others dislike it. Above the Fray Yet, these criticisms against the mainstream analysis of the sound of music should not be mistakenly regarded as a total rejection of its usefulness but serve to reveal to us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of sound (from the perspective of culture with sound, harmonic series, and musical culture as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. In addition, this case study of sound, harmonic series, and musical culture can teach us something valuable about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness- relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the order-chaos principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution-transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness-hardness principle, the seriousness-playfulness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 169 For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute tendency of those who are fun with harmonic series in music to focus on the combination of sound waves which are “consonant”), there is relativeness (e.g., what is beautiful for the fans of harmonic music to focus on consonant sounds is not necessarily so for the fans of John Cage, who prefer chaos and chance in music instead). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g., the predictable tendency of consonant sounds to be produced when they are “composite waves with short fundamental frequencies and shared or closely related partials”), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task to predict exactly which particular cultures in future eras will appreciate consonant sounds, under what occassions, etc.). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g., the explanation that sound waves which are “consonant” are therefore “pleasant,” as opposed to those dissonant ones which are “unpleasant” to hear), there is inexplicability (e.g., the lack of sufficient explanation, within this view, of why “consonant” sounds in music are necessarily “pleasant” and “dissonant” ones are necessarily “unpleasant,” as some people, for instance, enjoy chaotic music). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the identification of the “[v]ariations in air pressure against the ear drum, and the subsequent physical and neurological processing and interpretation,” as the origination of “the subjective experience called sound”), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the identification, since it is not clear how and why exactly a given sound is to be “interpreted” in different cultures and “sensitive” to different individuals). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relative simple nature of sine waves), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated nature of other waves which are “modelled by many different sine waves” of different “appropriate frequencies and amplitudes”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of the correlation between consonant sound waves and pleasant sounds), there is hiddneness (e.g., the hidden bias in the exploration of this correlation between consonant sound waves and The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 170 pleasant sounds, because it downgrades “dissonant” sound waves as “unpleasant”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of people who like harmonic series to find consonant sounds pleasant), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more empty, concentration of people who, like Cage, prefers chaotic music to find consonant sounds pleasant). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the order-chaos principle, if there is order (e.g., the relatively orderly patterns of harmonic series, like the “combination of composite waves with short fundamental frequencies and shared or closely related partials”), there is chaos (e.g., the relatively disorderly nature of chaotic music by Cage, with the use of chance in I Ching and sometimes dice and coin too). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relatively more developed ability of a musical composer of harmonic series to make use of consonant sounds), there is contraction (e.g., the relatively less developed ability of a musical composer of harmonic series to make use of dissonant sounds). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of harmonic series), there is praxis (e.g,. the practical application of harmonic series to the clinical use of music for musical therapy). (WK 2010u) And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional wisdom about consonant sounds as pleasant for beautiful music), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to this conventional wisdom about pleasant consonant sounds, by Cage with his new view that chaotic music can be beautiful too). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g,. the natural evolution of humans to be sensitive to different sounds in the state of nature), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human ability to listen to sounds by the invention of chaotic music, like the one by Cage). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the co-existence of different overtones), there is asymmetry (e.g., some overtones are harmonic—whereas others are inharmonic, because they are “created that are not anywhere near a harmonic”). And the reverse direction also holds true. Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 171 In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., consonant sounds), there is hardness (e.g., dissonant sounds). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the seriousness-playfulness principle, if there is seriousness (e.g., the serious nature of chaotic music for a different musical sensibility), there is playfulness (e.g., the playful nature of chaotic music when it plays with chance in the composition). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by harmonic music, as shown in the criticisms by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by harmonic music for the cultivation of pleasant consonant sounds). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values, regardless of whether this be done by way of harmonic music or chaotic music), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of harmonic music for a more conservative aesthetic experience—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of chaotic music for a more radical aesthetic experience). And the reverse direction also holds true. Sound, and �oise Aesthetics Another way to evaluate the possibility and desirability of sound from the perspective of culture has to do with sound and noise aesthetics. Definitions I use the term “noise aesthetics” here to relate it to the historical phenomenon of the exploitation of sound (especially noise) for music, also known as “noise music,” which refers to the “varieties of avant-garde music and sound art that may use elements such as cacophony, dissonance, atonality, noise, indeterminacy, and repetition in their realization.” (WK 2010ee) Noise music so defined “can feature distortion, various types of acoustically or electronically generated noise, randomly produced electronic signals, and non-traditional musical instruments. Noise music may also incorporate manipulated recordings, static, hiss and hum, feedback, live machine sounds, custom noise software, circuit bent The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 172 instruments, and non-musical vocal elements that push noise towards the ecstatic.” (WK 2010ee; T. Sangild 2002; C. Kelly 2009) However, the term “noise music” has been defined in different ways over time. For instance, “Ben Watson…points out that Ludwig van Beethoven’s Grosse Fuge (1825) 'sounded like noise' to his audience at the time. Indeed, Beethoven’s publishers persuaded him to remove it from its original setting as the last movement of a string quartet. He did so, replacing it with a sparkling Allegro. They subsequently published it separately.” (2010ee; B. Watson 2009) In a similar tone, Paul Hegarty (2007) “cites the work of noted cultural critics Jean Baudrillard, Georges Bataille and Theodor Adorno and through their work traces the history of 'noise.' He defines noise at different times as 'intrusive, unwanted,' 'lacking skill, not being appropriate' and 'a threatening emptiness.' He traces these trends starting with 18th century concert hall music. Hegarty contends that it is John Cage's composition 4'33", in which an audience sits through four and a half minutes of 'silence' (Cage 1973), that represents the beginning of noise music proper. For Hegarty, 'noise music,' as with 4'33", is that music made up of incidental sounds that represent perfectly the tension between 'desirable' sound (properly played musical notes) and undesirable 'noise' that make up all noise music from Erik Satie to NON to Glenn Branca.” (WK 2010ee) Douglas Kahn (1999), on the other hand, “discusses the use of noise as a medium and explores the ideas of Antonin Artaud, George Brecht, William Burroughs, Sergei Eisenstein, Fluxus, Allan Kaprow, Michael McClure, Yoko Ono, Jackson Pollock, Luigi Russolo, and Dziga Vertov.” (WK 2010ee) And Jacques Attali (1985) “explores the relationship between noise music and the future of society. He indicates that noise in music is a predictor of social change and demonstrates how noise acts as the subconscious of society—validating and testing new social and political realities.” (WK 2010ee; A. Weiss 1995) Characteristics With these different definitions in mind—noise music has distinctive characteristics. For illustration, consider a few of them below, as summarized in Table 2.6. Firstly, one major characteristic of noise music is that it gives noise a more positive evaluation in the context of aesthetics via music (than is the case in traditional melodic music). Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 173 For instance, “[i]n music, dissonance is the quality of sounds which seems 'unstable,' and has an aural 'need' to 'resolve' to a 'stable' consonance. Despite the fact that words like 'unpleasant' and 'grating' are often used to describe the sound of harsh dissonance, in fact all music with a harmonic or tonal basis—even music which is perceived as generally harmonious—incorporates some degree of dissonance.” (WK 2010ee) By contrast, relatively speaking of course, in traditional melodic music, noise has a negative connotation. For instance, “the word noise means unwanted sound or noise pollution. In electronics noise can refer to the electronic signal corresponding to acoustic noise (in an audio system) or the electronic signal corresponding to the (visual) noise commonly seen as 'snow' on a degraded television or video image. In signal processing or computing it can be considered data without meaning; that is, data that is not being used to transmit a signal, but is simply produced as an unwanted by-product of other activities. Noise can block, distort, or change the meaning of a message in both human and electronic communication. White noise is a random signal (or process) with a flat power spectral density. In other words, the signal contains equal power within a fixed bandwidth at any center frequency. White noise is considered analogous to white light which contains all frequencies.” (WK 2010ee; E. Hecht 2001; UCB 2010) And secondly, another major characteristic of noise music is that it makes good use of different technologies for noise creation. For instance, “[i]n much the same way the early modernists were inspired by naïve art, some contemporary digital art noise musicians are excited by the archaic audio technologies such as wire-recorders, the 8- track cartridge, and vinyl records. Many artists not only build their own noise-generating devices, but even their own specialized recording equipment and custom software (for example, the C++ software used in creating the viral symphOny by Joseph Nechvatal).” (WK 2010ee; S. Pedersen 2007; A. Observatori 2008) Historical Examples These different definitions and characteristics of noise music give us a general idea of noise music, which can be further illustrated by some historical examples as they have been created over time, as shown below (and summarized in Table 2.6). (a) The Art of Noises The first historical example of noise music has to do with “the art of noises.” (WK 2010ee) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 174 For instance, “Luigi Russolo, a futurist artist of the very early 20th century, was perhaps the first noise artist. His 1913 manifesto, L'Arte dei Rumori, translated as The Art of �oises, stated that the industrial revolution had given modern men a greater capacity to appreciate more complex sounds. Russolo found traditional melodic music confining and envisioned noise music as its future replacement. He designed and constructed a number of noise-generating devices called Intonarumori and assembled a noise orchestra to perform with them. A performance of his Gran Concerto Futuristico (1917) was met with strong disapproval and violence from the audience, as Russolo himself had predicted. None of his intoning devices have survived, though recently some have been reconstructed and used in performances. Although Russolo's works bear little resemblance to modern noise music, his pioneering creations cannot be overlooked as an essential stage in the evolution of this genre.” (WK 2020ee; L. Russolo 1986; P. Hegarty 2007) At the beginning, for Russolo (1986), “the art of music sought purity, limpidity and sweetness of sound. Then different sounds were amalgamated, care being taken, however, to caress the ear with gentle harmonies. Today music, as it becomes continually more complicated, strives to amalgamate the most dissonant, strange and harsh sounds. In this way we come ever closer to noise-sound.” (WK 2010ee) (b) Found Sound The second historical example of noise music has to do with “found sound.” (WK 2010ee) In the early 20th century, the “found sound” movement had different pioneers. For instance, there was “Parade, a performance produced at the Chatelet Theatre, Paris, on May 18, 1917, that was conceived by Jean Cocteau, with design by Pablo Picasso, choreography by Leonid Massine, and music by Eric Satie. The extra-musical materials used in the production were referred to as trompe l'oreille sounds by Coctueau and included a dynamo, Morse code machine, sirens, steam engine, airplane motor, and typewriters.” (WK 2010ee; J. Chadabe 1996) Then, “Arseny Avraamov's composition Symphony of Factory Sirens involved navy ship sirens and whistles, bus and car horns, factory sirens, cannons, foghorns, artillery guns, machine guns, hydro-airplanes, a specially designed steam-whistle machine creating noisy renderings of Internationale and Marseillaise for a piece conducted by a team using flags and pistols when performed in the city of Baku in 1922.” (WK 2010ee; M. Callanan 2010) Later, in 1923, “Arthur Honegger created Pacific 231, a modernist musical composition that imitates the sound of a steam locomotive. Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 175 Another example is Ottorino Respighi's 1924 orchestral piece Pines of Rome, which included the phonographic playback of a nightingale recording.” (WK 2010ee; J. Chadabe 1996; D. Albright 2004) At about the same time, in 1924, “George Antheil created a work entitled Ballet Mécanique with instrumentation that included 16 pianos, 3 airplane propellers, and 7 electric bells. The work was originally conceived as music for the Dada film of the same name, by Dudley Murphy and Fernand Léger, but in 1926 it premiered independently as a concert piece.” (WK 2010ee; J. Chadabe 1996) And in 1930, “Paul Hindemith and Ernst Toch recycled records to create sound montages and in 1936 Edgard Varese experimented with records, playing them backwards, and at varying speeds. Varese had earlier used sirens to create what he called a 'continuous flowing curve' of sound that he could not achieve with acoustic instruments. In 1931 Varese's Ionisation for 13 players featured 2 sirens, a lions's roar, and used 37 percussion instruments to create a repertoire of unpitched sounds making it the first musical work to be organized solely on the basis of noise. In remarking on Varese's contributions the American composer John Cage stated that Varese had 'established the present nature of music' and that he had 'moved into the field of sound itself while others were still discriminating 'musical tones' from noises.'” (WK 2010ee; R. Rice 2010; M. Nyman 1974) (c) Experimental Music The third historical example of noise music has to do with “experimental music.” (WK 2010e) For instance, “[i]n the 1940s,…[u]nder the influence of Henry Cowell in San Francisco, Lou Harrison and John Cage began composing music for 'junk' percussion ensembles, scouring junkyards and Chinatown antique shops for appropriately-tuned brake drums, flower pots, gongs, and more.” (WK 2010ee; H.
