Cowell 2004) Later, “[i]n late 1947 Antonin Artaud (1995) recorded Pour en Finir avec le Jugement de Dieu (To Have Done with the Judgment of god), an audio piece full of the seemingly random cacophony of xylophonic sounds mixed with various percussive elements, mixed with the noise of alarming human cries, screams, grunts, onomatopoeia, and glossolalia….Also in 1949, Boulez befriended John Cage, who was visiting Paris to do research on the music of Erik Satie. John Cage had been pushing music in even more startling directions during the war years, writing for prepared piano, junkyard percussion, and electronic gadgetry.” (WK 2010ee; P. Hegarty 2007; A. Ross 2007) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 176 (d) Postmodern Developments The fourth historical example of noise music has to do with “postmodern developments.” (WK 2010ee) Perhaps, the art critic Rosalind Krauss said it best when he “argued that by 1968 artists such as Robert Morris, Robert Smithson, and Richard Serra had 'entered a situation the logical conditions of which can no longer be described as modernist.' Sound art found itself in the same condition, but with an added emphasis on distribution. Antiform process art became the terms used to describe this post-modern post-industrial culture and the process by which it is made. Serious art music responded to this conjuncture in terms of intense noise, for example the La Monte Young Fluxus composition 89 VI 8 C. 1:42–1:52 AM Paris Encore from Poem For Chairs, Tables, Benches, Etc. Young's composition Two Sounds (1960) was composed for amplified percussion and window panes and his Poem for Tables, Chairs and Benches (1960) used the sounds of furniture scraping across the floor.” (WK 2010ee; R. Krauss 1986) (e) Industrial Music The fifth historical example of noise music has to do with “industrial music.” (WK 2010e) For instance, “[i]n the 1970s, the concept of art itself expanded and groups like Survival Research Laboratories, Borbetomagus and Elliott Sharp embraced and extended the most dissonant and least approachable aspects of these musical/spatial concepts. Around the same time, the first postmodern wave of industrial noise music appeared with Throbbing Gristle, Cabaret Voltaire, and NON (aka Boyd Rice). These cassette culture releases often featured zany tape editing, stark percussion and repetitive loops distorted to the point where they may degrade into harsh noise.” (WK 2010ee; R. Young 2009) Then, both in the 1970s and 1980s, “industrial noise groups like Current 93, Hafler Trio, Throbbing Gristle, Coil, Laibach, Steven Stapleton, Thee Temple ov Psychick Youth, Smegma, Nurse with Wound, Einstürzende Neubauten, The Haters, and The New Blockaders performed industrial noise music mixing loud metal percussion, guitars, and unconventional 'instruments' (such as jackhammers and bones) in elaborate stage performances. These industrial artists experimented with varying degrees of noise production techniques.” (WK 2010ee; B. Duguid 1995) And other examples include “Conceptual Art and the Neo-Dada [which] use of techniques such as assemblage, montage, bricolage, and appropriation.” (WK 2010ee) Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 177 (f) Noise Rock and No Wave Music The sixth historical example of noise music has to do with “noise rock and no wave music.” (WK 2010ee) For instance, “[t]he aptly-named noise rock fuses rock to noise, usually with recognizable 'rock' instrumentation, but with greater use of distortion and electronic effects, varying degrees of atonality, improvisation, and white noise. One notable band of this genre is Sonic Youth who took inspiration from the No Wave composers Glenn Branca and Rhys Chatham (himself a student of LaMonte Young).” (WK 2010ee) And “Marc Masters, in his book on the no wave, points out that aggressively innovative early dark noise groups like Mars and DNA drew on punk rock, avant-garde minimalism and performance art. Important in this noise trajectory are the nine nights of noise music called �oise Fest that was organized by Thurston Moore of Sonic Youth in the NYC art space White Columns in June 1981, followed by the Speed Trials noise rock series organized by Live Skull members in May 1983.” (WK 2010ee; M. Masters 2007; R. Young 2009) (g) Post-Industrial and Post-Digital Music And the seventh historical example of noise music has to do with “post-industrial and post-digital music.” (WK 2010ee) For instance, “there has been a flood of noise musicians whose ambient, microsound, or glitch-based work is often subtler to the ear. Kim Cascone refers to this development as a postdigital movement and describes it as an 'aesthetic of failure'….Goodman characterizes this widespread outpouring of free noise based media as a 'noise virus.'” (WK 2010ee; C. Kelly 2009; K. Cascone 2002; S. Goodman 2009) Others like “Richie Hawtin, Jan Jelinek, Ricardo Villalobos, Decomposed Subsonic, Trentemøller, and other Minimal techno and Microhouse DJs have been using noise elements such as buzz, hum, and clicks as sonic flavor since the early 1990s.” (WK 2010ee; S. Goodman 2009) Problems with �oise Aesthetics Yet, noise aesthetics has alos been subject to a lot of criticisms. For illustration, consider a few examples below, as summarized in Table 2.6. Firstly, one major criticism of noise aesthetics is that it celebrates a mixture of whatever techniques and tools available to make new kinds of noise, to the point that it can easily degenerate into the vice of what I originally called “irreverent eclecticism” in Chapter 4 of The Future of Human Civilization. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 178 Charles Baudelaire aptly observed about the dark side of eclecticism, when he wrote that “[e]clecticism has at all periods and places held itself superior to past doctrines because, coming last onto the scene, it finds the remotest horizons already open to it; but this impartiality only goes to prove the impotence of the eclectics. People who are so lavish with their times for reflection are not complete man: they lack the element of passion. No matter how clever he may be, an eclectic is but a feeble man; for he is a man without love. Therefore he has no ideal...; neither star nor compass. Doubt has led certain artists to beg the aid of all the other arts. Experiment with contradictory means, the encroachment of one art upon another, the importation of poetry, wit, and sentiment into painting—all these modern miseries are vices peculiar to the eclectics.” (P. Baofu 2000: 370; H. Janson 1995:888) And secondly, another major criticism of noise aesthetics is that it does not have universal appeal. For instance, those who favor hamornic music dislike noise aesthetics, as shown in the previous section on harmonic series. Here is a battle between the two camps in the history of music, the conservative for harmony and the radical for dissonance. More on this issue was already analyzed in my other books like The Future of Aesthetic Experience (2007) and The Future of Human Civilization (2000). A �ote of Caution Of course, these criticisms against noise aesthetics should not be misconstrued as a total dismissal of its usefulness but are to show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of sound (from the perspective of culture with sound and noise aesthetics as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. Furthermore, this case study of sound and noise aesthetics can cast an illuminating light on the nature of ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness-relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability- inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the change-constancy principle, the order-chaos principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory- praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution- transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness- Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 179 hardness principle, the seriousness-playfulness principle, the regression- progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute view of Russolo that “found traditional melodic music confining and envisioned noise music as its future replacement”), there is relativeness (e.g., what is appealing for Russolo in regard to noise music is not necessary so for the defenders of traditional melodic music who prefer harmonic series). In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g., the predictability of those in post-industrial and post- digital music like “Richie Hawtin, Jan Jelinek, Ricardo Villalobos, Decomposed Subsonic, Trentemøller, and other Minimal techno and Microhouse DJs” to use “noise elements such as buzz, hum, and clicks as sonic flavor since the early 1990s”), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task to predict exactly how long and to what extent this use of “buzz, hum, and clicks as sonic flavor” will last in which particular future eras). In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g., the explanation by those in noise music that dissonance is a desirable quality for music), there is inexplicability (e.g,. the lack of sufficient explanation, by those in noise music, of why dissonance is necessarily desirable for music, since, for the critics, its positive evaluation is not universal). In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise classification of some techniques which are central for industrial music, like “assemblage, montage, bricolage, and appropriation”), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the classification, since it is not clear why only techniques like these aforecited, not some others, are included). In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., at the beginning in the older days, the art of noises tended to be simple, pure, and sweet), there is complicatedness (e.g., nowadays, the art of noises “becomes continually more complicated, strives to amalgamate the most dissonant, strange and harsh sounds”). In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of sound for music), there is hiddenness (e.g., the hidden bias in sound music, because of its obsession with noise and dissonance, for instance). In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of noise musicians in the second half of the 20th century in the West), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 180 less dense, or more empty, concentration of noise musicians in the second half of the 20th century in Communist China and the Soviet Union). In relation to the change-constancy principle, if there is change (e.g., the ever new ways to do noise music, as shown in the seven historical examples), there is constancy (e.g., the ever constancy of the appeal of noise as a basis for music for some individuals). In relation to the order-chaos principle, if there is order (e.g., the relatively orderly nature of harmonic series in traditional melodic music), there is chaos (e.g., the relatively chaotic nature of dissonance in noise music). In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relative rise of the influence of noise music in the West, especially though not exclusively during the 20th century), there is contraction (e.g., the relative decline of the influence of traditional melodic music in the West especially in the 20th century). In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of “airplane propellers” in aeronautics), there is praxis (e.g., the practical application of the sound of “airplane propellers” to the field of “found sound” in noise music). In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional wisdom in traditional music, about the distinction between “musical tones” and “noise”), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to this conventional wisdom about music by Varese in found music, who proposed a new way of doing music, that is, by incorporating noise into music itself). In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to hear sounds in the state of nature), there is transformation (e.g,. the technical transformation of human ability to hear sounds by the invention of different musical instruments, like those used by noise music as a modern addition). In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the existence of different genres of music), there is asymmetry (e.g., traditional melodic music focuses on harmonic series—but noise music focuses on dssonance). In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., the pleasant sounds in harmonic series), there is hardness (e.g., “the most dissonant, strange and harsh sounds” in the contemporary art of noises). In relation to the seriousness-playfulness principle, if there is seriousness (e.g., the serious business by those in noise music to create a new kind of music), there is playfulness (e.g., the playful nature by those Chapter 2: Sound and Its Doubleness 181 in noise music to play with different techniques and instruments in the process of creating new music). In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the progression made by noise music, as shown in the criticisms by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by noise music for a new way to appreciate noise in music). And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values, regardless of whether this be done by way of traditional melodic music or noise music), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of traditional melodic music for a more conservative musical lifestyle—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of noise music for a more radical musical lifestyle). And the reverse direction also holds true. The Disturbance of Sound This comprehensive analysis of the possibility and desirability of sound, from the perspectives of the mind, nature, society, and culture, is to show us the different ways in which sound is both possible and desirable, but not to the extent that the spokespersons from each side would like us to believe. Sound thus has its disturbance, just as it has its orderliness too, as the other side of the same coin. But this is only one part of a larger story, since there is the other side of the story, which concerns silence, the opposite of sound. Since this chapter already analyzes sound, the next chapter will therefore deal with the issue of silence. The importance of these dual analyses should not be underestimated, because those on the side of sound often treat silence merely as the opposite of sound without really appreciating it from the standpoint of silence too. With this in mind, let’s now turn to Chapter Three for the study of silence and its duality—for which we now turn to chapter three. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 182 Table 2.1. See book for citations. • PART THREE • _____________________________________ Silence CHAPTER 3 SILE�CE A�D ITS DUALITY _____________________________________ There is a silence where hath been no sound, There is a silence where no sound may be,—In the cold grave, under the deep, deep sea, Or in the wide desert where no life is found. —Thomas Hood (BT 2010c) The Serenity of Silence Acoustics deals with the study of both sound and silence (which is “the relative or total lack of audible sound,” dependent on the sound perception of an organic species or an electrical equipment)—as already analyzed in Sec. 1.2. This relationship between sound and silence is true, even though silence does not always have to be an absolute lack of audible sound, so the distinction between sound and silence can be one of degree. That said—any study of sound requires an exploration of the nature of silence too, as one cannot be completely disconnected from the other. With this in mind, this book offers a dialectic treatment of sound and silence in that, if sound has its orderliness, it has its disturbance too—just as, if silence has its serenity, it likewise has its turrnoil. The inquiry concernng silence is the subject matter of this chapter (Chapter Two), whereas that of sound was already addressed in Chapter Two. Besides, the relationship between sound and silence constitutes a scholarly challenge, in that one cannot analyze silence (or sound, for that matter) completely separately. Consequently, this then means that the issues concerning silence in this chapter (Chapter Three) and sound in Chapter Three can overlap, as each issue on one can be relevant to the other too. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 192 With this clarification in mind—a good way to examine the duality of silence is by way of the evaluation of the extent to which it (silence) is in fact both possible and desirabe. This chapter thus takes the challenging task to provide a comprehensive analysis of silence in relation to acoustics from the four perspectives of the mind, nature, society, and culture (in accordance to my sophisticated methodological holism, as explained in Sec. 1.8). Thus, this chapter is organized in four main sections, in relation to (3.2) silence and the mind, (3.3) silence and nature, (3.4) silence and society, and (3.5) silence and culture—to be analyzed hereafter, respectively (and summarized in Table 3.1). Silence and the Mind Silence, when examined from the perspective of the mind, can reveal something fascinating about its possibility and desirability, and this can be shown by way of two case studies, namely, (3.2.1) silence, deafness, and the mask of benevolence and (3.2.2) silence, stuttering, and speech disorder—to be addressed below, in that order. Silence, Deafness, and the Mask of Benevolence The word “deafness” (also known as “hearing impairment,” “hearing loss,” or “hard of hearing”) refers to “conditions in which individuals are fully or partially unable to detect or perceive at least some frequencies of sound which can typically be heard by members of their species.” (WK 2010v) However, some deaf people do not like the term “impaired” to be applied to them; instead, they prefer the terms “deaf” and “hard of hearing,” for instance. (WK 2010v) On Definition The first issue to deal with hearing impairment is about its definition, in relation to the test of hearing sensitivity. Hearing sensitivity is often correlated with the way that “animals use sound to communicate,” and therefore “hearing in that type of animal is most sensitive for the frequencies produced by calls, or in the case of humans, speech.” (WK 2010v) So, to define “hearing impairment” is to identify “when an animal has diminished sensitivity to the sounds normally heard by its species. In Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 193 humans, the term hearing impairment is usually reserved for people who have relative insensitivity to sound in the speech frequencies. The severity of a hearing impairment is categorized according to the increase in volume that must be made above the usual level before the listener can detect it. In profound deafness, even the loudest sounds that can be produced by an audiometer (an instrument used to measure hearing) may not be detected.” (WK 2010v) An alternative definitional concern has to do with to “the perceived clarity of a sound rather than its amplitude. In humans, that aspect is usually measured by tests of speech perception. These tests measure one's ability to understand speech, not to merely detect sound. There are very rare types of hearing impairments which affect speech understanding alone.” (WK 2010v) On Classification The second issue to deal with hearing impairment is about its classification into four major categories, namely, (a) by type, (b) by severity, (c) by age of onset, and (d) by number of impaired ears, as described below (and summarized in Table 3.2). (a) By Type Hearing impairment can be classified by type, which can be “conductive, sensorineural, or both.” (WK 2010v) In regard to the first type, “a conductive hearing impairment is an impairment resulting from dysfunction in any of the mechanisms that normally conduct sound waves through the outer ear, the eardrum or the bones of the middle ear.” (WK 2010v) In regard to the second type, “[a] sensorineural hearing impairment is one resulting from dysfunction in the inner ear, especially the cochlea where sound vibrations are converted into neural signals, or in any part of the brain that subsequently processes these signals….Sensorineural loss…is by far the most common type of hearing loss.” (WK 2010v) And in regard to the third type, some individuals have the misfortune to suffer from both, not just from conductive or sensorineural hearing impairment. (b) By Severity Hearing impairment can be classified by severity, which “is ranked according to the loudness (measured in decibels (dB)) a sound must be before being detected by an individual. Hearing impairment may be ranked as mild, moderate, severe or profound as defined below”: (WK 2010v) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 194 • “Mild” –“for adults: between 27 and 40 dB” –“for children: between 20 and 40 dB” • “Moderate” –“between 41 and 55 dB” • “Moderately Severe” –“between 56 and 70 dB” • “Severe” –“between 71 and 90 dB” • “Profound” –“90 dB or greater” However, “[f]or certain legal purposes such as insurance claims, hearing impairments are described in terms of percentages….[T]he idea of a percentage of hearing loss is somewhat arbitrary, but where decibels of loss are converted via a recognized legal formula, it is possible to calculate a standardized 'percentage of hearing loss' which is suitable for legal purposes only.” (WK 2010v) Another way to classify severity is “a Speech-in-Noise test. As the name implies, a Speech-in-Noise test will give you an indication of how well you can understand speech in a noisy environment. A person with a hearing loss will often be less able to understand speech, especially in noisy conditions.” (WK 2010v) (c) By Age of Onset Hearing impairment can be classified by age of onset, in terms of two main types, namely, “pre-lingual deafness” and “post-lingual deafness.” (WK 2010v) In regard to “pre-lingual deafness”—the hearing impairment “is sustained prior to the acquisition of language, which can occur as a result of a congenital condition or through hearing loss in early infancy. Prelingual deafness impairs an individual's ability to acquire a spoken language, but children born into signing families rarely have delays in language development. Most pre-lingual hearing impairment is acquired via either disease or trauma rather than genetically inherited, so families with deaf children nearly always lack previous experience with sign language.” (WK 2010v) And in regard to “post-lingual deafness”—the hearing impairment “is sustained after the acquisition of language, which can occur as a result of disease, trauma, or as a side-effect of a medicine. Typically, hearing loss is gradual and often detected by family and friends of affected individuals long before the patients themselves will acknowledge the disability. Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 195 Common treatments include hearing aids and learning lip reading.” (WK 2010v) In general, “post-lingual deafness is far more common than pre- lingual deafness.” (WK 2010v) (d) By Number of Impaired Ears Hearing impairment can be classified by number of impaired ears, namely, either “unilateral” or “bilateral.” (WK 2010v) In regard to “unilateral” hearing impairment—the hearing impairment is called “single sided deafness/SSD” and has “an impairment in only one ear. This can impair a person's ability to localize sounds (e.g., determining where traffic is coming from) and distinguish sounds from background noise in noisy environments.” (WK 2010v) And in regard to “bilateral” hearing impairment—the hearing impairment has an impairment in two ears. On Causes The third issue to deal with hearing impairment is about its classification into different causes, namely, (a) by age, (b) by long-term exposure to environmental noise, (c) by genetics, (d) by disease or illness, (e) by medications, (f) by exposure to ototoxic chemicals, and (g) by physical trauma, as described below (and summarized in Table 3.2). (a) By Age Hearing impairment can be classified in terms of its cause by age. For instance, “presbycusis, the progressive loss of ability to hear high frequencies with increasing age, begins in early adulthood, but does not usually interfere with ability to understand conversation until much later.” (WK 2010v) (b) By Long-Term Exposure to Environmental Noise Hearing impairment can be classified in terms of its cause by long- term exposure to environmental noise. For instance, “[p]opulations of people living near airports or freeways are exposed to levels of noise typically in the 65 to 75 dB(A) range. If lifestyles include significant outdoor or open window conditions, these exposures over time can degrade hearing.” (WK 2010v) (b) By Genetics Hearing impairment can be classified in terms of its cause by genetics. For instance, “[i]f a family has a dominant gene for deafness it will persist across generations because it will manifest itself in the offspring even if it is inherited from only one parent. If a family had genetic hearing The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 196 impairment caused by a recessive gene it will not always be apparent as it will have to be passed onto offspring from both parents.” (WK 2010v) (d) By Disease or Illness Hearing impairment can be classified in terms of its cause by disease or illness. For example, any of the following diseases or illnesses can have negative impact on hearing: Measles, Meningitis, Autoimmune disease, Mumps (Epidemic parotitis), Presbycusis, Adenoids, AIDS, HIV, Chlamydia, Fetal alcohol syndrome, Syphilis, Otosclerosis, etc. (WK 2010v) (e) By Medications Hearing impairment can be classified in terms of its cause by medications. For instance, “[s]ome medications cause irreversible damage to the ear, and are limited in their use for this reason. The most important group is the aminoglycosides (main member gentamicin) and platinum based chemotherapeutics such as cisplatin. Various other medications may reversibly affect hearing. This includes some diuretics, aspirin and NSAIDs, and macrolide antibiotics.” (WK 2010v) (f) By Exposure to Ototoxic Chemicals Hearing impairment can be classified in terms of its cause by exposure to ototoxic chemicals. For instance, any of the following ototoxic chemicals can have negative impact on hearing: (WK 2010v) • “Drugs”—“antimalarial, antibiotics, anti-inflammatory (non- steroidal), antineoplastic, diuretics” • “Solvents”—“toluene, styrene, xylene, n-hexane, ethyl benzene, white spirits/Stoddard, carbon disulfide, fuels, perchloroethylene, trichloroethylene, p-xylene” • “Asphyxiants”—“carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide” • “Metals”—“lead, mercury, organotins (trimethyltin)” • “Pesticides/Herbicides”—“paraquat, organophosphates” Surely, the list is not complete but illustrative only. (g) By Physical Trauma Hearing impairment can be classified in terms of its cause by physical trauma, especially in relation to the “damage either to the ear itself or to the brain centers that process the aural information conveyed by the ears.” (WK 2010v) For instance, “people who sustain head injury are especially vulnerable to hearing loss or tinnitus, either temporary or permanent,” and Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 197 “exposure to very loud noise (90 dB or more, such as jet engines at close range) can cause progressive hearing loss. Exposure to a single event of extremely loud noise (such as explosions) can also cause temporary or permanent hearing loss. A typical source of acoustic trauma is an excessively loud music concert.” (WK 2010v) On Treatment The fourth issue to deal with hearing impairment is about its classification into different types of treatment, namely, (a) by approaches, (b) by gene therapy, (c) by assistive techniques and devices, and (d) by resources and interventions, as described below (and summarized in Table 3.2). (a) By Approaches The treatment of hearing impairment can be classified in terms of different approaches. For instance, “[i]f the hearing loss occurs at a young age, interference with the acquisition of spoken language and social skills may occur. Hearing aids, which amplify the incoming sound, may alleviate some of the problems caused by hearing impairment, but are often insufficient. Cochlear implants artificially stimulate the VIIIth Nerve by providing an electric impulse substitution for the firing of hair cells.” (WK 2010v) (b) By Gene Therapy The treatment of hearing impairment can be classified in terms of gene therapy. For instance, “a 2008 study has shown that gene therapy targeting Atoh1 can cause hair cell growth and attract neuronal processes in embryonic mice. It is hoped that a similar treatment will one day ameliorate hearing loss in humans.” (WK 2010v) (c) By Assistive Techniques and Devices The treatment of hearing impairment can be classified in terms of different assistive techniques and devices. For instance, any of the following techniques and devices can assist those who suffer from hearing impairment: (WK 2010v) • “Individuals can communicate by telephone using Telecommunications Device for the Deaf (TDD). These devices look like typewriters or word processors and transmit typed text over regular telephone lines. Other names in common use are textphone and minicom.” The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 198 • “Mobile textphone devices came onto the market as of 2004, allowing simultaneous two way text communication.” • “Videophones and similar video technologies can be used for distance communication using sign language. Video conferencing technologies permit signed conversations as well as permitting a sign language- English interpreter to voice and sign conversations between a hearing impaired person and that person's hearing party, negating the use of a TTY device or computer keyboard.” • “Video Relay Service and Video Remote Interpreting services also use a third-party telecommunication service to allow a deaf or hard- of-hearing person to communicate quickly and conveniently with a hearing person, through a sign language interpreter.” • “Hearing dogs are a specific type of assistance dog specifically selected and trained to assist the deaf and hearing impaired by alerting their handler to important sounds, such as doorbells, smoke alarms, ringing telephones, or alarm clocks.” • “Other assistive devices include those that use flashing lights to signal events such as a ringing telephone, a doorbell, or a fire alarm.” • “The advent of the Internet's World Wide Web and closed captioning has given the hearing impaired unprecedented access to information. Electronic mail and online chat have reduced the need for deaf and hard-of-hearing people to use a third-party Telecommunications Relay Service in order to communicate with the hearing and other hearing impaired people.” Of course, there can be other techniques and devices, so the list above is illustrative only. (d) By Resources and Interventions The treatment of hearing impairment can be classified in terms of different resources and interventions. For instance, there are “wireless devices” like “the FM system, the audio induction loop and the infra red system. Each system has advantages and benefits for particular uses.” (WK 2010v) In addition, “[i]nside the classroom, children with hearing impairments may also benefit from interventions. These include providing favorable seating for the child. This can be done by having the student sit as close to the teacher as possible so that they will be able to hear the teacher, or read the teacher's lips more easily….When teaching students with hearing impairments, try to use overheads as much as possible. Overheads allow the teacher to write, as well as maintain visual focus on the hearing impaired student. For those students who are completely deaf, Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 199 one of the most common interventions is having the child communicate with others through an interpreter using sign language.” (WK 2010v; UIUC 2010) Problems in Dealing with Hearing Impairment But these different ways to deal with hearing impairment are not without their own problems. Consider, for illustration, some major problems below. Firstly, one major problem in dealing with hearing impairment is that it can be costly. For instance, “Cochlear implants are not only expensive, but require sophisticated programming in conjunction with patient training for effectiveness.” (WK 2010v) It is thus not surprising that “[t]here has been considerable controversy within the culturally Deaf community over cochlear implants,” especially when there are “the chances of a head injury, which carries a greater risk where the implant is involved.” (WK 2010v) Secondly, another major problem in dealing with hearing impairment is that there is no guarantee for success. For instance, in regard to gene therapy, “it is important to note, however, that the regrowth of cochlear hair cells does not imply the restoration of hearing sensitivity as the sensory cells may or may not make connections with neurons that carry the signals from hair cells to the brain.” (WK 2010v) Thirdly, still another major problem in dealing with hearing impairment is that the aid to those who suffer from hearing impairment can degenerate into a new kind of patronizing and oppressive maltreatment of them, as pointed out by the critics, like Harlan Lane (1992:48-9) in his 1992 book titled The Mask of Benevolence. And fourthly, one more major problem in dealing with hearing impairment is that, contrary to the popular belief in mainstream society, “[i]n Deaf culture, deafness is not considered a condition that needs to be fixed” and is not regarded as “a pathological condition, viewing it instead as a locus of pride.” (WK 2010y; P. Ladd 2003; A. Mindess 2006) A Didactic Exercise These problems in dealing with hearing-impaired people do not mean to dismiss the usefulness of the different treatments but to show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of silence (from the perspective of the mind with silence, deafness, and the The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 200 mask of benevolence as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. More importantly, the analysis of silence, deafness, and the mask of benevolence can reveal the relevance of the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness- relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the change-constancy principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution-transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness-hardness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute concern, in a definition of hearing impairment, with hearing sensitivity), there is relativeness (e.g., what is the right concern with hearing sensitivity in a definition of hearing impairment is not necessarily so for those who focus on hearing clarity in an alternative definition). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g., the predictable tendency of those who accept gene therapy to seek the regrowth of cochlear hair cells), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task to predict exactly which particular gene therapy will be successful, under what conditions, since “the restoration of hearing sensitivity as the sensory cells may or may not make connections with neurons that carry the signals from hair cells to the brain”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g,. the explanation by those who care for deaf people that hearing impairment is something to be corrected for the elimination or reduction of their suffering), there is inexplicability (e.g,. the lack of convincing explanation, within this assertive view, of why their care is necessarily needed, since, contrary to the popular view in mainstream society, “[i]n Deaf culture, deafness is not considered a condition that needs to be fixed” and is not regarded as “a pathological condition, viewing it instead as a locus of pride.”) And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise classification of the five types of severity in hearing impairment measurement, namely, “mild,” “moderate,” Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 201 “moderately severe,” “severe,” and “profound”), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the classification, since it is not clear why there are only five types, not four, six, seven, etc.). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple analysis of deafness in terms of the major issues as described above), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated analysis of deafness by questioning the assumptions and claims in regard to the major issues as described above, as shown in the criticisms by the critics). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of the need for society to aid hearing-impaired people), there is hiddenness (e.g., the hidden bias in this social aid to hearing-impaired people, since it often degenerate into a new kind of patronizing and oppressive maltreatment of them, as what Lane called “the mask of benevolence”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser, or more pervasive, spread of people with normal hearing in society), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more empty, spread of hearing-impaired people in society). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the change-constancy principle, if there is change (e.g. the ever new ways for hearing-impaired people to be treated), there is constancy (e.g., the ever constant existence of ways for hearing-impaired people to be treated). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower speed of people to have hearing loss by long- term exposure to environmental noise like living near airports or freeways), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively faster speed of people to have hearing loss by head injury in an explosion). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relatively more developed ability of those hearing–impaired people who solicit the help of others in society to seek different assistive techniques, resources, and intervention), there is contraction (e.g., the relatively less developed ability of those hearing–impaired people who solicit the help of others in society to counter the patronizing mask of benevolence from society, as pointed out by Lane). And the reverse direction also holds true. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 202 In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of genetics), there is praxis (e.g., the practical application of genetics to the field of hearing impairment for gene therapy). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional wisdom that hearing-impaired people need help from others and society in general), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to this conventional wisdom about the benevolent help of society, by the new view that this help often degenerates into a new kind of patronizing and oppressive maltreatment of them, as what Lane called “the mask of benevolence”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to suffer from hearing loss in the state of nature), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human ability to counter hearing loss by the invention of gene therapy, among other methods). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the co-existence of different individuals in society), there is asymmetry (e.g., some individuals have severe hearing loss—but some other individuals do not have severe hearing loss). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., the benevolence of those who care about hearing-impaired people), there is hardness (e.g., the mask of benevolence of those who care about hearing-impaired people, as pointed out by Lane). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by the different treatments of hearing loss, as shown in the criticisms by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by the different treatments of hearing loss for the improvement of hearing). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and control of beliefs and behaviors, regardless of whether this be done by way of social help to deaf people or self-help instead), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and control of beliefs and behaviors by way of social help to deaf people for a relatively more cooperative society—but the contribution to the molding and control of beliefs and behaviors by way of self-help for a relatively more competitive society). And the reverse direction also holds true. Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 203 Silence, Stuttering, and Speech Disorder Another way to evaluate the possibility and desirability of silence from the perspective of the mind has to do with silence, stuttering, and speech disorder. The Issue of Definition The term “stuttering” (also known as “stammering”) refers to “a speech disorder in which the flow of speech is disrupted by involuntary repetitions and prolongations of sounds, syllables, words or phrases, and involuntary silent pauses or blocks in which the stutterer is unable to produce sounds.” (WK 2010w) In popular usage, “the term 'stuttering'…covers a wide spectrum of severity: it may encompass individuals with barely perceptible impediments, for whom the disorder is largely cosmetic, as well as others with extremely severe symptoms, for whom the problem can effectively prevent most oral communication.” (WK 2010w) However, the tem “stuttering” should not be confused with the related term “developmental stuttering,” which refers to “stuttering that originates when a child is learning to speak and develops as the child matures into adulthood. Other speech disorders with symptoms resembling stuttering are cluttering, Parkinson's speech, essential tremor, palilalia, spasmodic dysphonia, selective mutism and social anxiety.” (WK 2010w) The Issue of Characteristics Stuttering can be described in terms of three major characteristics, namely, (a) primary behaviors, (b) variability, and (c) feelings and attitudes—to be addressed in what follows (and summarized in Table 3.3). (a) Primary Behaviors The first major characteristic of stuttering concerns its “primary behaviors,” which “are the overt, observable signs of speech fluency breakdown, including repeating sounds, syllables, words or phrases, silent blocks and prolongation of sounds. These differ in from the normal disfluencies found in all speakers in that stuttering disfluencies may last longer, occur more frequently, and are produced with more effort and strain.” (WK 2010w; D. Ward 2006) In general, stuttering has three distinct symptoms, as shown below. (WK 2010w) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 204 • “Repetition”—“occurs when a unit of speech, such as a sound, syllable, word, or phrase is repeated and are typical in children who are beginning to stutter. For example, 'to-to-to-tomorrow.'” (WK 2010w) • “Prolongations”—“are the unnatural lengthening of continuant sounds, for example, 'mmmmmmmmmilk.' Prolongations are also common in children beginning to stutter.” (WK 2010w) • “Blocks of Silence”—“are inappropriate cessation of sound and air [silence], often associated with freezing of the movement of the tongue, lips and/or vocal folds. Blocks often develop later, and can be associated with muscle tension and effort.” (WK 2010w; B. Guitar 2005) Besides these three characteristics, stuttering also differs in terms of severity. (b) Variability The second major characteristic of stuttering concerns its variability (or severity), because “[t]he severity of a stutter is often not constant even for severe stutterers. Stutterers commonly report dramatically increased fluency when talking in unison with another speaker, copying another's speech, whispering, singing, and acting or when talking to pets, young children, or themselves. Other situations, such as public speaking and speaking on the telephone are often greatly feared by stutterers, and increased stuttering is reported.” (WK 2010w; D. Ward 2006) (c) Feelings and Attitudes The third major characteristic of stuttering concerns feelings and attitudes, because “stuttering may have a significant negative cognitive and affective impact on the stutterer.” (WK 2010w) For isntance, “Joseph Sheehan, a prominent researcher in the field, has described stuttering in terms of the well-known analogy to an iceberg, with the immediately visible and audible symptoms of stuttering above the waterline and a broader set of symptoms such as negative emotions hidden below the surface. Feelings of embarrassment, shame, frustration, fear, anger, and guilt are frequent in stutterers, and may actually increase tension and effort, leading to increased stuttering.” (WK 2010w; J. Kalinowski 2006; D. Ward 2006; B. Guitar 2005) Over time, “continued exposure to difficult speaking experiences may crystallize into a negative self-concept and self-image. A stutterer may project his or her attitudes onto others, believing that they think he or she is nervous or stupid. Such negative feelings and attitudes may need to be a Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 205 major focus of a treatment program. Many stutterers report about a high emotional cost, including jobs or promotions not received, as well as relationships broken or not pursued.” (WK 2010w; A. Pollack 2006; B. Guitar 2005) The Issue of Causes Stuttering can be explained in terms of three major causes, namely, (a) metabolic, (b) developmental, and (c) acquired—to be addressed in what follows, respectively (and summarized in Table 3.3). (a) Metabolic The first major cause of stuttering is “metabolic” (or genetic), because “[s]ome inherited forms of stuttering have been traced to variations in genes governing lysosomal metabolism.” (WK 2010w; NEJM 2010) Gerald Maguire at the University of California, Irvine claimed that “[t]his builds upon the belief that has been growing over the last 10 years that stuttering is not a behavioral disorder, but a genetic disorder with manifestation in the brain,” (WK 2010w; SM 2010) (b) Developmental The second major cause of stuttering is “development,” not “genetic,” in that it can be cured, in certain cases. For instance, “[s]tuttering is…a developmental disorder beginning in early childhood and continuing into adulthood in at least 20% of affected children.” (WK 2010w; N. Gordon 2002; A. Craig 2005) Although in cases like this, “the rate of early recovery is very high”— “with time a young stutterer may transition from easy, relaxed repetition to more tense and effortful stuttering, including blocks and prolongations. Some propose that parental reaction may affect the development of chronic stutter. Recommendations to slow down, take a breath, say it again, etc. may increase the child’s anxiety and fear, leading to more difficulties with speaking and, in the 'cycle of stuttering' to ever yet more fear, anxiety and expectation of stuttering.” (WK 2010w; N. Gordon 2002; D. Ward 2006) (c) Acquired The third major cause of stuttering is “acquired,” due to some unexpected events in life. For instance, “[i]n rare cases, stuttering may be acquired in adulthood as the result of a neurological event such as a head injury, tumour, stroke or drug use. The stuttering has different characteristics from its developmental equivalent: it tends to be limited to part-word or sound The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 206 repetitions, and is associated with a relative lack of anxiety and secondary stuttering behaviors. Techniques such as altered auditory feedback, which may promote fluency in stutterers with the developmental condition, are not effective with the acquired type.” (WK 2010w; N. Gordon 2002; D. Ward 2006; A. Craig 2005) The Issue of Treatment Stuttering can be treated in six major ways, namely, (a) fluency shaping therapy, (b) stuttering modication therapy, (c) electronic fluency devices, (d) anti-stuttering medications, (e) support groups and the self- help movement, and (f) diaphragmatic breathing—to be addressed hereafter, in that order (and summarized in Table 3.3). (a) Fluency Shaping Therapy The first major treatment of stuttering makes use of “fluency shaping therapy” (also known as “speak more fluently,” “prolonged speech” or “connected speech”), which “trains stutterers to speak fluently by controlling their breathing, phonation, and articulation (lips, jaw, and tongue). It is based on operant conditioning techniques.” (WK 2010w; D. Ward 2006) In this therapy, “[s]tutterers are trained to reduce their speaking rate by stretching vowels and consonants, and using other fluency techniques such as continuous airflow and soft speech contacts. The result is very slow, monotonic, but fluent speech used only in the speech clinic. After the stutterer masters these fluency skills, the speaking rate and intonation are increased gradually….Fluency shaping approaches are often taught in intensive group therapy programs, which may take two to three weeks to complete, but more recently the Camperdown program…us[es] a much shorter schedule….” (WK 2010w; D. Ward 2006) (b) Stuttering Modification Therapy The second major treatment of stuttering makes use of “stuttering modification therapy,” which “is not to eliminate stuttering but to modify it so that stuttering is easier and less effortful. The rationale is that since fear and anxiety causes increased stuttering, using easier stuttering and with less fear and avoidance, stuttering will decrease. The most widely known approach was published by Charles Van Riper in 1973 and is also known as block modification therapy.” (WK 2010w; D. Ward 2006) (c) Electronic Fluency Devices The third major treatment of stuttering makes use of “electronic fluency devices,” which provide “altered auditory feedback, so that Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 207 stutterers hear their voice differently” and “have been used for over 50 years in the treatment of stuttering.” (WK 2010w; A. Bothe 2007) However, “[s]tudies of these techniques have had mixed results, with some stutterers showing substantial reductions in stuttering, while others improved only slightly or not at all. In a 2006 review of the efficacy of stuttering treatments, none of the studies on altered auditory feedback met the criteria for experimental quality, such as the presence of control groups.” (WK 2010w; A. Bothe 2006 &2007) (d) Anti-Stuttering Medications The fourth major treatment of stuttering makes use of “anti-stuttering medicaitons,” like “benzodiazepines, anti-convulsants, anti-depressants, antipsychotic and antihypertensive medications, and dopamine antagonists.” (WK 2010w) However, “[a] comprehensive review of pharmacological treatments of stuttering in 2006 concluded that few of the drug trials were methodologically sound. Of those that were, only one, not unflawed study, showed a reduction in the frequency of stuttering to less than 5% of words spoken. In addition, potentially serious side effects of pharmacological treatments were noted, such as weight gain and the potential for blood pressure increases.” (WK 2010w; G. Maguire 2000; A. Bothe 2006) (e) Support Groups and the Self-Help Movement The fifth major treatment of stuttering makes use of “support groups and the self-help movement,” which “gain popularity and support by professionals and people who stutter. One of the basic tenets behind the self-help movement is that since a cure does not exist, quality of living can be improved by improved acceptance of self and stuttering.” (WK 2010w) (f) Diaphragmatic Breathing And the sixth major treatment of stuttering makes use of “diaphragmatic breathing,” which is “costal breathing…as a means by which stuttering can be controlled.” (WK 2010w) Problems in Dealing with Stuttering However, these different treatments are not without their own problems. Consider, for illustration, a few of them below. Firstly, one major criticism against these different treatments is that they do not completely restore or create speech naturalness. For instance, in regard to “fluency shaping therapy”— the “lack of speech naturalness at the end of treatment remains a frequent criticism.” The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 208 (WK 2010w) And in regard to “anti-stuttering medications”—“few of the drug trials were methodologically sound.” (WK 2010w) Secondly, another major criticism against these different treatments is that they have negative side-effects. For instance, in regard to “anti-stuttering medications”—“serious side effects of pharmacological treatments were noted, such as weight gain and the potential for blood pressure increases.” (WK 2010w; G. Maguire 2000; A. Bothe 2006) And thirdly, still another major criticism against these different treatments is that they can be time-consuming. For instance, in regard to the “fluency shaping therapy”—although the training programs can take only a few weeks in the speech clinic, the exercise can continue outside the speech clinic after the patient resumes his daily life in society. Going Further Of course, these criticisms against the different treatments of stuttering do not imply their utter uselesness but only show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of silence (from the perspective of the mind with silence, stuttering, and speech disorder as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. In addition, the analysis of silence, stuttering, and speech disorder can teach us something valuable about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness- relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the change-constancy principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution-transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness-hardness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute concern, of some parents, with stuttering in their children, such that they encourage the children “to slow down, take a breath, say it again, etc.” as a way to resolve the problem), there is relativeness (e.g., what is the right thing to do for some parents who encourage their children “to slow down, take a breath, say it again, etc.” as a way to resolve the problem is not necessarily so for the children Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 209 who suffer from stuttering, because this encouragement can instead “increase the child’s anxiety and fear, leading to more difficulties with speaking and, in the 'cycle of stuttering' to ever yet more fear, anxiety and expectation”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g., the predictable tendency of a stutterer to receive any of the six major treatments), there is unpredictability (e.g, the more difficult task to predict exactly which treatment will yield success to a given stutterer under what conditions, since there are problems in the treatments, as shown in the criticisms by the critics). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g., the explanation, by those in support groups and the self- help movement, that, since “existing behavioral, prosthetic, and pharmaceutical treatments provid[e]…limited relief from the overt symptoms of stuttering” and “since a cure does not exist, quality of living can be improved by improved acceptance of self and stuttering”), there is inexplicability (e.g., the lack of convincing explanation, by those in support groups and the self-help movement, of why self-help is the way to go or is better, simply because existing treatments provide only limited relief and a cure does not really exist, since, for the critics, it is questionable if self-help can do much of anything under these circumstances). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise classification of the three major characteristics of stuttering), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the classification of the three major characteristics of stuttering, since it is not clear why there are only three characteristics, not four, five, six, and so on). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple recommendation, by the advocates, of the six different treatments for stuttering), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated analysis of the six different treatments for stuttering by questioning their claims and assumptions, as shown in the criticisms by the critics). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., “the immediately visible and audible symptoms of stuttering” as the portion of an iceberg above the waterline, according to the analogy by Joseph Sheehan), there is hiddenness (e.g., “a broader set of symptoms The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 210 such as negative emotions hidden below the surface” of the iceberg, as an analogy by Sheehan). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of individuals who prefer “anti- stuttering medications” as a treatment of stuttering to use “benzodiazepines, anti-convulsants, anti-depressants, antipsychotic and antihypertensive medications, and dopamine antagonists,” for instance), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more empty, concentraton of individuals who prefer support groups and the self-help movement to use anti-stuttering medications). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the change-constancy principle, if there is change (e.g., the ever new ways to treat stuttering, as shown in the six different treatments proposed over time), there is constancy (e.g., the ever constant existence of ways to treat stuttering). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower speed of traditional group therapy programs for fluency shaping therapy to complete, since they normally take “two to three weeks to complete”), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively faster speed of the more recent Camperdown program for fluency shaping therapy to complete, since they “use a much shorter schedule” than the traditional group therapy programs). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relative spread of the influence of “support groups and the self- help movement” nowadays), there is contraction (e.g., the relatively decline of the influence of traditional “behavioral, prosthetic, and pharmaceutical treatments” nowadays, because they “provid[e]…limited relief from the overt symptoms of stuttering”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of electronic devices for auditory purposes in electronical engineering), there is praxis (e.g, the practical application of electronic engineering to the field of stuttering for electronic fluency devices as a treatment of stuttering). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional wisdom of treating stuttering “around eighteenth and nineteenth century Europe,” like “cutting the tongue with scissors, removing a triangular wedge from the posterior tongue, and cutting Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 211 nerves, or neck and lip muscles”), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to the conventional wisdom of treating stuttering, by the six new ways of treating stuttering nowadays). (WK 2010w) And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to have some members suffering from stuttering in primitive times), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human ability to treat stuttering by the invention of “anti-stuttering medications” and “electronic fluency devices” for the treatment). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the co-existence of different stutterers in society), there is asymmetry (e.g., some stutterers have only “barely perceptible impediments, for whom the disorder is largely cosmetic”—but other stutterers have “extremely severe symptoms, for whom the problem can effectively prevent most oral communication”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., the parental support of stutterers by encouragin them “to slow down, take a breath, say it again, etc.”), there is hardness (e.g., the making fun of the stutterers by others). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by different treatments of stuttering, as shown in the criticisms by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by different treatments of stuttering, as shown by the “relief from the overt symptoms of stuttering”). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors, regardless of whether this be done by way of the treatment of stuttering or by way of the acceptance of stuttering), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of the treatment of stuttering for the cultivation of more polished civil manners—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of the acceptance of stuttering for the tolerance of more impulsive civil manners). And the reverse direction also holds true. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 212 Silence and �ature Silence, when examined from the perspective of nature, can reveal in an amazing way its possibility and desirability, and this can be done by way of a fascinating case study, namely, silence, infrasound, animals, and ghosts—to be addressed below. Silence, Infrasound, Animals, and Ghosts A fascinating way to evaluate the possibility and desirability of silence from the perspective of nature has to do with silence, infrasound, animals, and ghosts. (as summarized in Table 3.4). Silence and Infrasound The word “infrasound” here refers to a “sound that is lower in frequency than 20 Hz (Hertz) or cycles per second, the 'normal' limit of human hearing,” which is why humans normally do not hear infrasound, as it becomes non-audible or silent to the human ears—except with the use of special equipments. (WK 2010x) In other words, “[h]earing becomes gradually less sensitive as frequency decreases, so for humans to perceive infrasound, the sound pressure must be sufficiently high. The ear is the primary organ for sensing infrasound, but at higher levels it is possible to feel infrasound vibrations in various parts of the body.” (WK 2010x) And “[t]he study of such sound waves is sometimes referred to as infrasonics, covering sounds beneath 20 Hz down to 0.001 Hz. This frequency range is utilized for monitoring earthquakes, charting rock and petroleum formations below the earth, and also in ballistocardiography and seismocardiography to study the mechanics of the heart. Infrasound is characterized by an ability to cover long distances and get around obstacles with little dissipation.” (WK 2010x) Infrasound and Animals In the state of nature, infrasound comes from different sources, be they in relation to natural events or to animals. For instance, in relation to natural events, “[i]nfrasound sometimes results naturally from severe weather, surf, lee waves, avalanches, earthquakes, volcanoes, bolides, waterfalls, calving of icebergs, aurorae, lightning and upper-atmospheric lightning. Nonlinear ocean wave interactions in ocean storms produce pervasive infrasound vibrations Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 213 around 0.2 Hz, known as microbaroms.” (WK 2010x; M. Garcesc 2003 & 2006; H. Haak 2006; UA 2010) And in relation to animals, “[w]hales, elephants, hippopotamuses, rhinoceros, giraffes, okapi, and alligators are known to use infrasound to communicate over distances—up to hundreds of miles in the case of whales. It has also been suggested that migrating birds use naturally generated infrasound, from sources such as turbulent airflow over mountain ranges, as a navigational aid.” (WK 2010x) The case of elephants is telling, because “[e]lephants, in particular, produce infrasound waves that travel through solid ground and are sensed by other herds using their feet, although they may be separated by hundreds of kilometres. These calls range from 15–35 Hz and can be as loud as 117 dB, allowing communication for many kilometres, with a possible maximum range of around 10 km (6 mi). These calls may be used to coordinate the movement of herds and allow male elephants to find mates.” (WK 2010x; W. Langbauer 1991; D. Larom 1997) In general, “[a]nimals have been known to perceive the infrasonic waves going through the earth by natural disasters and can use these as an early warning. A recent example of this is the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami. Animals were reported to flee the area long before the actual tsunami hit the shores of Asia. It is not known for sure if this is the exact reason, as some have suggested that it was the influence of electromagnetic waves, and not of infrasonic waves, that prompted these animals to flee.” (WK 2010x; C. Kenneally 2004; PBS 2005) Infrasound and Ghosts Even more fascinatingly, the study of infrasound in nature can explain something about “ghosts” or “supernatural beings.” To start, it is important to explain the unusualness of infrasound, which is often inaudible to humans, because “20 Hz is considered the normal low frequency limit of human hearing”—unless some special equipments are used. (WK 2010x) However, this can be qualified, because, under some ideal conditions, for instance, “[w]hen pure sine waves are reproduced under ideal conditions and at very high volume, a human listener will be able to identify tones as low as 12 Hz. Below 10 Hz it is possible to perceive the single cycles of the sound, along with a sensation of pressure at the eardrums.” (WK 2010x; H. Olson 1967) That said—“combined with the natural spread in thresholds within a population, it may have the effect that a very low frequency sound which is inaudible to some people may be loud to others. Infrasound has been The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 214 known to cause feelings of awe or fear in humans. Since it is not consciously perceived, it can make people feel vaguely that supernatural events are taking place. Some film soundtracks make use of infrasound to produce unease or disorientation in the audience. Irréversible is one such movie, as is Paranormal Activity.” (WK 2010x; MSNBC 2007) Precisely here in this context, infrasound has been used to explain the phenomena of “ghosts.” For instance, “[r]esearch by Vic Tandy, a lecturer at Coventry University, suggested that an infrasonic signal of 19 Hz might be responsible for some ghost sightings. Tandy was working late one night alone in a supposedly haunted laboratory at Warwick, when he felt very anxious and could detect a grey blob out of the corner of his eye. When Tandy turned to face the grey blob, there was nothing.” (WK 2010x) Then, in the next day, “Tandy was working on his fencing foil, with the handle held in a vise. Although there was nothing touching it, the blade started to vibrate wildly. Further investigation led Tandy to discover that the extractor fan in the lab was emitting a frequency of 18.98 Hz, very close to the resonant frequency of the eye given as 18 Hz by NASA. This was why Tandy had seen a ghostly figure—it was an optical illusion caused by his eyeballs resonating. The room was exactly half a wavelength in length, and the desk was in the centre, thus causing a standing wave which was detected by the foil.” (WK 2010x; SD 2010) After this experience, “Tandy investigated this phenomenon further and wrote a paper entitled The Ghost in the Machine. Tandy carried out a number of investigations at various sites believed to be haunted, including the basement of the Tourist Information Bureau next to Coventry Cathedral and Edinburgh Castle.” (WK 2010x; V. Tandy 1998 & 2000; C. Arnot 2000; S. Dudman 2003; IAWM 2007) Problems with the Studies However, there are problems with these studies. Consider, for illustration, a few of them below, as summarized in Table 3.4. Firstly, one major criticism against the studies is that the explanations may not be true. For instance, in regard to animals, the allegation about the use of infrasound to predict disaster remains to be proved, because “[i]t is not known for sure if this is the exact reason, as some have suggested that it was the influence of electromagnetic waves, and not of infrasonic waves, that prompted these animals to flee.” (WK 2010x; C. Kenneally 2004; PBS 2005) Secondly, another major criticism against the studies is that there are alternative explanations instead. For instance, in regard to the phenomenon Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 215 of ghosts (or supernatural events), Tandy’s explanation is not satisfactory because it tries to explain away the existence of “ghosts” as “an optical illusion”; but, for the critics (or believers of anomalous expereince), there is something more than just “an optical illusion” in anomalous experience like “ghosts” (or “supernatural beings”). And thirdly, still another major criticism against the studies is that the explanation explains the wrong phenomenon. For instance, in regard to the phenomenon of ghosts (or supernatural events), Tandy’s explanation, for the critics, is not really about “ghosts,” but about something which sounds like “ghosts.” Transcending the Debate Once again, these criticisms against the studies do not mean to dismiss their validity outright but only show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of silence (from the perspective of nature with silence, infrasound, animals, and ghosts as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. More importantly, the analysis of silence, infrasound, animals, and ghosts reveals something vital about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the formalness- informalness principle, the absoluteness-relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness- complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution-transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness-hardness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the formalness-informalness principle, if there is formalness (e.g., the formal logical requirement of completeness in scientific work, like the research on animals using infrasound to predict disaster), there is informalness (e.g., the non-formal existence of incompleteness in the research on animals using infrasound to predict disaster, because “[i]t is not known for sure if this is the exact reason, as some have suggested that it was the influence of electromagnetic waves, and not of infrasonic waves, that prompted these animals to flee”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute advantage of elephants to sense infrasound The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 216 waves produced at a distance of hundreds of kilometres), there is relativeness (e.g., what is possible for elephants to hear infrasound waves produced at a distance of hundreds of kilometres is not so for humans, because “20 Hz is considered the normal low frequency limit of human hearing,” and also not at a distance of hundreds of kilometres away). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is prediction (e.g., the predictable tendency of someone like Tandy to claim that ghost sightings are optical illusions), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task for Tandy to predict exactly what particular ghosts, not just illusive or apparent ghostly figures, will be sighted whenever infrasound is emitted). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g., the explanation, by the advocates, that some animals can use infrasound to predict disaster), there is inexplicability (e.g., the lack of sufficient explanation, within this view, of why this must be true, since “some have suggested that it was the influence of electromagnetic waves, and not of infrasonic waves, that prompted these animals to flee”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise identification of a distance of “several hundreds of kilometres” away that elephants can hear infrasound), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the identification, since it is not clear exactly how many kilometres away the elephants can hear infrasound). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple analysis of ghost sightings as optical illusions by Tandy), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated analysis of ghost sightings as optical illusions by questioning the assumptions and claims used by Tandy, as shown in the criticisms by the critics). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of the relationship between ghost sightings and optical illusions by Tandy), there is hiddenness (e.g., the hidden bias in Tandy’s research, because of his obsession with apparent ghostly figures under the conditions that he encountered, which are not the same of ghosts in the literature of anomalous experience). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of animals to be able to naturally hear infrasound over distances), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 217 dense, or more empty, concentration of humans to be able to naturally hear infrasound over distances, without the help of special equipments). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower speed of humans “to flee the area long before the actual tsunami hit the shores” during the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively quicker speed of animals “to flee the area long before the actual tsunami hit the shores” in the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relative expansion of the influence of science in trying to explain ghost sightings nowadays), there is contraction (e.g., the relative decline of the influence of esoteric religion to explain ghost sightings nowadays). And the reverse direction also holds true.
