In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of infrasound in infrasonics), there is praxis (e.g., the practical application of infrosonics to the field of nuclear weapons, as “the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization uses infrasound as one of its monitoring technologies”). (WK 2010x) And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional view about “ghosts” in esoteric religion), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to the conventional wisdom about “ghosts” in esoteric religion, by Tandy’s new view that ghost sightings are optical illusions). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to be unable to naturally hear infrasound at low frequences), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human ability to hear infrasound at low frequences by the invention of special equipments as in ballistocardiography and seismocardiography). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., both humans and animals have hearing ability), there is asymmetry (e.g., “sound that is lower in frequency than 20 Hz (Hertz) or cycles per second” is “the 'normal' limit of human hearing”—but elephants can hear sounds at frequencies lower than 20 Hz). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., some sounds are pleasant for humans to hear, as in hamonic music), there The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 218 is hardness (e.g., some sounds cause “feelings of anxiety or fear in humans” to hear, as in infrasound). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by Tandy’s work on ghost sightings, as shown in the criticisms by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by Tandy’s work for a new way to understand ghost sightings). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values, regardless of whether this be done by way of science or by way of esoteric religion, both in regard to the research on ghost sightings), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of science for a more secular worldview—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of esoteric religion for a more sacred worldview). And the reverse direction also holds true. Silence and Society Silence, when examined from the perspective of society, can cast an illuminating light on its possibility and desirability, and this can be shown by way of two case studies, namely, (3.4.1) silence, noise-control, and architectural acoustics, and (3.4.2) silence, the law, and the right to quiet enjoyment—to be addressed below, respectively. Silence, �oise-Control, and Architectural Acoustics The term “architectural acoustics,” as already defined in Sec. 1.4, refers to “the science of noise control within buildings.” (WK 2010f) In fact, “he first application of architectural acoustics was in the design of opera houses and then concert halls. More widely, noise suppression is critical in the design of multi-unit dwellings and business premises that generate significant noise, including music venues like bars. The more mundane design of workplaces has implications for noise health effects. Architectural acoustics includes room acoustics, the design of recording and broadcast studios, home theaters, and listening rooms for media playback.” (WK 2010f) Consider, for illustration, four major ways that architectural acoustics are applied in society for noise-control, namely, (a) building skin envelope, (b) inter-space noise control, (c) interior space acoustics, and (d) Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 219 mechanical equipment noise—to be addressed below, in that order (and summarized in Table 3.5). Building Skin Envelope The first illustration of the application of architectural acoustics to noise control in society has to do with “building skin envelope.” (WK 2010f) The term “building skin envelope” refers to a “science” which “analyzes noise transmission from building exterior envelope to interior and vice versa. The main noise paths are roofs, eaves, walls, windows, door and penetrations. Sufficient control ensures space functionality and is often required based on building use and local municipal codes.” (WK 201f) For instance, this science becomes necessary when working on “a suitable design for a home which is to be constructed close to a high volume roadway, or under the flight path of a major airport, or of the airport itself.” (WK 2010f) Inter-Space �oise Control The second illustration of the application of architectural acoustics to noise control in society has to do with “inter-space noise control.” (WK 2010f) The term “inter-space noise control” refers to a “science” which analyzes “limiting and/or controlling noise transmission from one building space to another to ensure space functionality and speech privacy. The typical sound paths are room partitions, acoustic ceiling panels (such as wood dropped ceiling panels), doors, windows, flanking, ducting and other penetrations.” (WK 2010f) For instance, this science becomes necessary when working on a “suitable party wall design in an apartment complex to minimise the mutual disturbance due to noise by residents in adjacent apartments.” (WK 2010f) Interior-Space Acoustics The third illustration of the application of architectural acoustics to noise control in society has to do with “interior-space acoustics.” (WK 2010f) The term “interior-space acoustics” refers to a “science” which analyzes “controlling a room's surfaces based on sound absorbing and The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 220 reflecting properties. Excessive reverberation time, which can be calculated, can lead to poor speech intelligibility.” (WK 2010f) The properties of “sound reflection” and “sound absorption are important enough. Firstly, in regard to “sound reflection”—it helps to “create standing waves that produce natural resonances that can be heard as a pleasant sensation or an annoying one. Reflective surfaces can be angled and coordinated to provide good coverage of sound for a listener in a concert hall or music recital space. To illustrate this concept consider the difference between a modern large office meeting room or lecture theater and a traditional classroom with all hard surfaces.” (WK 2010f; G. Ballou 1998) Secondly, in regard to “sound absorption”—it helps to absorb unwanted sound for noise control. For instance, “[i]nterior building surfaces can be constructed of many different materials and finishes. Ideal acoustical panels are those without a face or finish material that interferes with the acoustical infill or substrate. Fabric covered panels are one way to heighten acoustical absorption. Finish material is used to cover over the acoustical substrate. Mineral fiber board, or Micore, is a commonly used acoustical substrate. Finish materials often consist of fabric, wood or acoustical tile. Fabric can be wrapped around substrates to create what is referred to as a 'pre-fabricated panel' and often provides the good noise absorption if laid onto a wall. Prefabricated panels are limited to the size of the substrate ranging from 2'x 4' to 4' x 10'. Fabric retained in a wall- mounted perimeter track system, is referred to as 'on-site acoustical wall panels.' This is constructed by framing the perimeter track into shape, infilling the acoustical substrate and then stretching and tucking the fabric into the perimeter frame system. On-site wall panels can be constructed to accommodate door frames, baseboard, or any other intrusion. Large panels (generally, greater than 50 square feet) can be created on walls and ceilings with this method. Wood finishes can consist of punched or routed slots and provide a natural look to the interior space, although acoustical absorption may not be great.” (WK 2010f) In any event, when interior-space acoustics is applied for noise control in workplace, there are three major ways to achieve the goal, also known as “the ABCs,” as shown below: (WK 2010f) • “A = Absorb {via drapes, carpets, ceiling tiles, etc.)” • “B = Block (via panels, walls, floors, ceilings and layout)” • “C = Cover-up (via sound masking)” Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 221 Of course, “[w]hile all three of these are recommended to achieve optimal results, C = Cover-up by increasing background sound produces the most dramatic improvement in speech privacy—with the least disruption and typically the lowest cost.” (WK 2010f) Mechanical Equipment �oise The fourth illustration of the application of architectural acoustics to noise control in society has to do with “mechanical equipment noise.” (WK 2010f) The term “mechanical equipment noise” refers to a “science” which analyzes “building services noise control” for “controlling noise produced by” mechanical equipments like the following: (WK 2010f) • “ACMV (air conditioning and mechanical ventilation) systems in buildings, termed HVAC in North America” • “Elevators” • “Electrical generators positioned within or attached to a building” • “Any other building service infrastructure component that emits sound” This kind of noise control is important, because “[i]nadequate control may lead to elevated sound levels within the space which can be annoying and reduce speech intelligibility. Typical improvements are vibration isolation of mechanical equipment, and sound traps in ductwork. Sound masking can also be created by adjusting HVAC noise to a predetermined level.” (WK 2010f) Problems with the Application of Architectural Acoustics But the application of architectural acoustics to noise control in society is not without its own problems. Consider, for illustration, a few of them below, as summarized in Table 3.5. Firstly, one major criticism of the application of architectural acoustics to the domain of noise control in society is that health effects from noise can be exaggerated to the point that other real concerns are neglected. For instance, “hearing loss could be attributed to a variety of factors including age, rather than solely due to excessive exposure to noise.” (WK 2010z; C. Schmidt 2005; S. Staples 1996) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 222 Secondly, another major criticism of the application of architectural acoustics to the domain of noise control in society is that government regulations are often not comprehensive enough and not fully enforceable. For instance, in the U.S., in spite of “the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) in 1969 and the Noise Pollution and Abatement Act, more commonly called the Noise Control Act (NCA), in 1972—even “the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) had testified before Congress that 30 million Americans are exposed to non- occupational noise high enough to cause hearing loss and 44 million Americans live in homes impacted by aircraft or highway noise.” (WK 2010aa; USSPWC 1972) In addition, “[m]any municipalities do not follow up on complaints. Even where a municipality has an enforcement office, it may only be willing to issue warnings, since taking offenders to court is expensive.” (WK 2010aa) Thirdly, still another major criticism of the application of architectural acoustics to the domain of noise control in society is that the different ways to conrol noise in society can be very costly. For instance, it is not surprising that “undeveloped countries” are too poor to be on the frontline of applying architectural acoustics for noise control in a comprehensive way and therefore often “lag…behind” in its application. (WK 2010aa) And fourthly, one more major criticism of the application of architectural acoustics to the domain of noise control in society is that not all cultures equally dislike noise to the same extent. For instance, in many Latin-American cultures, the lifestyle is often noisier, be it about how people live together or how they have fun— relatively speaking of course, when compared with those in a Buddhist monastery. Maneuvering between Two Opposing Sides Once more, these criticisms against the application of architectural acoustics to the domain of noise control in society do not mean to totally reject its usefulness but only show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of silence (from the perspective of nature with silence, noise control, and architectural acoustics as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. Furthermore, the analysis of silence, noise control, and architectural acoustics can teach us something valuable about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness- Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 223 relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution-transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness-hardness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute concern of those in “building skin envelope” with “noise transmission from building exterior envelope to interior and vice versa,” like working on “a suitable design for a home… close to a high volume roadway, or under the flight path of a major airport”), there is relativeness (e.g., what is the right focus for those in “building skin envelope” is not necessarily so for those in “mechanical equipment noise,” who are more concerned with mechanical equipments like “air conditioning and mechanical ventilation systems in buildings,” “elevators,” etc.). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g., the predictable tendency of government regulaion in the U.S. nowadays for noise control), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task to predict exactly to what extent government regulations will be comprehensive enough and fully enforceable, because of the continued problems with government regulations, as shown in the criticisms by the critics). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g., the explanation by those in architectural acoustics that noise control is necessary to minimize negative health effects from noise), there is inexplicability (e.g., the lack of sufficient explanation, within this view, of why noise control is really so important, since, for the critics, other real concerns are neglected, because “hearing loss could be attributed to a variety of factors including age, rather than solely due to excessive exposure to noise”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise classification of three major ways to achieve noise control in workplace, namely, “the ABCs”), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the classification, since it is not clear why there are only three major ways, not four, five, six, and so on). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple analysis of the four applications of The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 224 architectural acoustics to the domain of noise control in society), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated analysis of the application of architectural acoustics to the domain of noise control in society by questioning its assumptions and claims, as shown in the criticisms by the critics). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of the relationship between architectural acoustics and the minimization of negative health effects from noise), there is hiddenness (e.g., the hidden bias in architectural acoustics, because of its questionable assumptions, as shown in the criticisms by the critics). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of government regulations in the U.S. for higher noise-control standards), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more empty, concentration of government regulations in “undeveloped countries” for higher noise standards). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower speed of European countries to set up noise- control standards nowadays, which “generally lag by 10 to 20 years,” when compared with those in the U.S.), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively faster speed of the U.S. to set up noise-control standards nowadays, which generally are ahead of European countries “by 10 to 20 years”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relative spread of government regulations for noise control in society nowadays, especially in the U.S.), there is contraction (e.g., the relative loss of the ability of citizens to engage in noisy activities nowadays without government regulations, especially in the U.S.). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of acoustics, especially in relation to sound absorption, sound reflection, and sound masking), there is praxis (e.g., the practical application of acoustics to the field of architecture for noise control). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional wisdom in the older days, for instance, “[i]n the 1960s and earlier,” when “few people recognized that citizens might be entitled to be protected from adverse sound level exposure”), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to this conventional wisdom about sound level exposure, by “the National Environmental Policy Act in Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 225 1969 and the Noise Pollution and Abatement Act, more commonly called the Noise Control Act, in 1972,” which set up government regulation for noise control). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to live in the state of nature, at times with unwanted noise), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human living together in society, by the invention of government regulation for noise control). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the co-existence of different government regulations in different countries), there is asymmetry (e.g., the noise-control standards in American government regulation are higher than European government regulation, with a gap “by 10 to 20 years”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., the making of pleasant sound), there is hardness (e.g., the making of annoying sound). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by architectural acoustics, as shown in the criticisms by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by architectural acoustics for noise control in society). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors, regardless of whether this be done by way of noise control through government regulation or by way of noise management through free market), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of noise control through government regulation for a relatively more powerful political society—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of noise management through free market for a relativley more powerful civil society). And the reverse direction also holds true. Silence, the Right to Quiet Enjoyment, and the Law Another way to evaluate the possibility and desirability of silence from the perspective of society has to do with silence, the right to quiet enjoyment, and the law. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 226 Definition The term “right to quiet enjoyment” is covered under “nuisance” in tort law (especially under the common law), which, as already defined in Sec. 1.4, refers to “that which causes offence, annoyance, trouble or injury,” in that “persons in possession of real property (land owners, lease holders etc.) are entitled to the quiet enjoyment of their lands.” (WK 2010g) But “this doesn't include visitors or those who aren't considered to have an interest in the land. If a neighbour interferes with that quiet enjoyment, either by creating smells, sounds, pollution or any other hazard that extends past the boundaries of the property, the affected party may make a claim in nuisance.” (WK 2010g) Under the common law, the term “nuisance” is used “in three ways,” as shown below: (WK 2010g) • “Activity or Condition”—“that is harmful or annoying to others (e.g., indecent conduct, a rubbish heap or a smoking chimney)” • “Harm”—that is “caused by the before-mentioned activity or condition (e.g., loud noises or objectionable odors)” • “Legal Liability”—“that arises from the combination of the two” And “a nuisance can be either public (also 'common') or private,” as described below: (WK 2010g) • “Public Nuisance”—refers to, as English scholar Sir J. F. Stephen defined it, “an act not warranted by law, or an omission to discharge a legal duty, which act or omission obstructs or causes inconvenience or damage to the public in the exercise of rights common to all His Majesty's subjects.” • “Private Nuisance”—refers to “the interference with the right of specific people,” which means “a violation of one's use of quiet enjoyment of land. It doesn't include trespass.” In other words, “[t]he law of nuisance was created to stop such bothersome activities or conduct when they unreasonably interfered either with the rights of other private landowners (i.e., private nuisance) or with the rights of the general public (i.e., public nuisance).” (WK 2010g) However, to avoid misunderstanding, there are three distinctions to be made hereafter. Firstly, one distinction to be clarified is that the “interference” in the definition “was not the result of a neighbor stealing land or trespassing on Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 227 the land,”which falls under the jursdiction of property law, not tort law. (WK 2010g; W. Prosser 1966) Secondly, another distinction to be clarified is that “the level of interference must rise above the merely aesthetic. For example: if your neighbour paints their house purple, it may offend you; however, it doesn't rise to the level of nuisance. In most cases, normal uses of a property that can constitute quiet enjoyment cannot be restrained in nuisance either. For example, the sound of a crying baby may be annoying, but it is an expected part of quiet enjoyment of property and does not constitute a nuisance.” (WK 2010g) And thirdly, still another distinction to be clarified is that “any affected property owner has standing to sue for a private nuisance. If a nuisance is widespread enough, but yet has a public purpose, it is often treated at law as a public nuisance. Owners of interests in real property (whether owners, lessors, or holders of an easement or other interest) have standing only to bring private nuisance suits.” (WK 2010g) With these distinctions in mind—“[n]uisance is one of the oldest causes of action known to the common law, with cases framed in nuisance going back almost to the beginning of recorded case law.” (WK 2010g) History of the Legal Development of �uisance At the beginning, especially “[i]n the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the law of nuisance became difficult to administer, as competing property uses often posed a nuisance to each other, and the cost of litigation to settle the issue grew prohibitive.” (WK 2010g) Because of this probem (among others), the law of nuisance becomes more complicated over time. Consider two examples below, for illustration. Firstly, one example is to distinguish the law of nuisance from zoning laws, because “most jurisdictions now have a system of land use planning (e.g. zoning) that describes what activities are acceptable in a given location. Zoning generally overrules nuisance. For example: if a factory is operating in an industrial zone, neighbours in the neighbouring residential zone can't make a claim in nuisance. Jurisdictions without zoning laws, essentially leave land use to be determined by the laws concerning nuisance.” (WK 2010g) Secondly, another example is to distinguish the law of nuisance from environmental laws, because “modern environmental laws are an adaptation of the doctrine of nuisance to modern complex societies, in that a person's use of his property may harmfully affect another's property, or The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 228 person, far from the nuisance activity, and from causes not easily integrated into historic understandings of nuisance law.” (WK 2010g) Remedies These distinctions aside—once nuisance suits are brought to court, the issue of “remedies” is important in disputes about nuisance, and the remedies can be in terms of monetary compensation (as in “money damages”) or of injunction (as in “equitable remedies”). (WK 2010g) For example, “under the common law, the only remedy for a nuisance was the payment of damages. However, with the development of the courts of equity, the remedy of an injunction became available to prevent a defendant from repeating the activity that caused the nuisance, and specifying punishment for contempt if the defendant is in breach of such an injunction.” (WK 2010g) This then gave rise to “[t]he law and economics movement,” which “has been involved in analyzing the most efficient choice of remedies given the circumstances of the nuisance. In Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co. a cement plant interfered with a number of neighbors, yet the cost of complying with a full injunction would have been far more than a fair value of the cost to the plaintiffs of continuation. The New York court allowed the cement plant owner to 'purchase' the injunction for a specified amount—the permanent damages. In theory, the permanent damage amount should be the net present value of all future damages suffered by the plaintiff.” (WK 2010g) And the person who is in charge of the official duty of making investigations about nuisance used to be called “the Inspector of Nuisance,” but this term is “now archaic,” because “the position and/or term having been replaced by others. For example, in the United Kingdom, this office was generally associated with public health and sanitation. Both the 1847 Nuisances Removal and Diseases Prevention Act and the Metropolis Management Act 1855 defined such an office. Similar offices were established across the British Empire. The nearest modern equivalent of this position in the UK is an Environmental health officer. In the United States, a modern example is found in Section 3767 of the Ohio Revised Code which defines such a position to investigate nuisances, where this term broadly covers establishments in which lewdness and alcohol are found.” (WK 2010g) Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 229 Problems with Public �uisance But there are problems with the enforcement of tort law in regard to nuisance (especially for “the right to quiet enjoyment”). Consider, for illustration, some of them below. Firstly, one major problem with the enforcement of tort law in regard to nuisance (especially for “the right to quiet enjoyment”) is that it can be very costly. For instance, “in Boomer v. Atlantic Cement Co.” (as mentioned above), “the cost of complying with a full injunction would have been far more than a fair value of the cost to the plaintiffs of continuation.” (WK 2010g) Secondly, another major problem with the enforcement of tort law in regard to nuisance (especially for “the right to quiet enjoyment”) is that it becomes more and more complicated, to the point that it often falls under the jurisdiction of other laws. For instance, the law of nuisance becomes overruled by other laws like “zoning laws” and “environmental laws” (as indicated above). Thirdly, still another major problem with the enforcement of tort law in regard to nuisance (especially for “the right to quiet enjoyment”) is that what counts as “damage” in tort law is subject to different contentious legal interpretations. (WK 2009) For instance, “damage” can be interpreted in different ways, be they physical, economc, emotional, reputational, etc.; this disagreement is further compounded, when, in some cases, the “damages…cannot be quantified exactly in monetary terms.” (WK 2009) And the same can be said about the interpretation of “the duty of care” which is important in judging any case of nuisance, since there are different answers, depending on different cases; after all, the “guidelines for the courts in establishing a duty of care” are not universal, as “much of the principle is still at the discretion of judges.” (WK 2009) This issue of legal interpretation was already extensively analyzed in another book of mine titled The Future of Post-Human Law (2010g). Looking Beyond These criticisms against the enforcement of “the right to quiet enjoyment” are not meant to imply the uselessness of the law of nuisance but only show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of silence (from the perspective of society with silence, the right to quiet enjoyment, and the law as a case study here) are The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 230 not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. In addition, the analysis of silence, the right to quiet enjoyment, and the law can reveal something insightful about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness- relativeness principle, the partiality-totality principle, the predictability- unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution-transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness-hardness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute tendency of a legal interpretation of what counts as “the duty of care” in tort law), there is relativeness (e.g., what counts as “the duty of care” by a judge in tort law is not necessarily so for another judge, because the “guidelines for the courts in establishing a duty of care” are not universal, as “much of the principle is still at the discretion of judges”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the partiality-totality principle, if there is partiality (e.g., the relatively partial view from the individual interests of each landowner to purse activities which benefit him), there is totality (e.g., the relativley holistic vew from the social interests of society as a whole, such that the whole is not the sum of its parts, in that society also creates the law of nuisance “to stop…bothersome activities or conduct when they unreasonably interfered either with the rights of other private landowners…or with the rights of the general public”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g. the predictable tendency of remedies to be settled on the basis of either monetary compensation, as in “money damages,” or of injunction, as in “equitable remedies”), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task to predict exactly beforehand what the outcome of a particular nuisance case will turn out to be, because the remedies can be in different ways, just as a given case may not lead to the consideration of remedies as a solution at all). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explanation (e.g, the explanation that the principle of “the duty of care” is vital for judging a nuisance case in relation to the right to quiet Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 231 enjoyment), there is inexplicability (e.g., the lack of sufficient explanation, within this view, of why the principle of “the duty of care” is the only one or the main one to be used in judging a nuisance case in the first place). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise identification of the issue of “damage” as important in judging the resolution of a nuisance case in common law), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the identification of the issue of “damage” in tort law, because in some cases, the “damages…cannot be quantified exactly in monetary terms,” and what counts as “damage” can be subject to different legal interpretations). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple nature of the law of nuisance at the beginning of its historical development), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated nature of the law of nuisance, especially after “the late 19th and early 20th centuries,” when “the law of nuisance became difficult to administer, as competing property uses often posed a nuisance to each other, and the cost of litigation to settle the issue grew prohibitive”; later, it was overruled or adapted by other laws like zoning laws and environmental laws). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of the relationship between the understanding of “the duty of care” in tort law and the legal interpretation of such an understanding), there is hiddenness (e.g., the hidden bias in a given legal interpretation, since, in the case about “the duty of care,” in general, “much of the principle is still at the discretion of judges”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of nuisance cases nowadays which are overruled or adapted by other laws like zoning laws and environmental laws), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more empty, concentration of nuisance cases nowadays which are totally independent of other laws like zoning laws and environmental laws). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower speed of a nuisance case to be accepted in court, if “the level of interference” with the rights of others does not rise “above the merely aesthetic”), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively quicker speed of a nuisance case to be accepted in court, if “the level of interference” The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 232 with the rights of others rises much “above the merely aesthetic”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relative spread, in our time, of the influence of “[t]he law and economics movement,” which “has been involved in analyzing the most efficient choice of remedies given the circumstances of the nuisance”), there is contraction (e.g., the relative decline, in our time, of the influence of religion in judging nuisance cases). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of efficiency in the law and economics movement), there is praxis (e.g., the practical application of efficiency in the law and economics movement to the field of tort law, like the case about the right to quiet enjoyment). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional wisdom in the older days when the law of nuisance was not closely related to other laws like zoning laws and environmental laws), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to this conventional wisdom nowadays, when the law of nuisance can be overruled and adapted by other laws like zoning laws and environmental laws). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to live together in the state of nature, with activities which sometimes annoy others), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human living together, by the invention of “the right to quiet enjoyment” in tort law which is to regulate activities which may annoy each other). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the existence of both private nuisance and public nuisance), there is asymmetry (e.g., “owners of interests in real property [whether owners, lessors, or holders of an easement or other interest] have standing only to bring private nuisance suits,” even when “a nuisance is widespread enough” to cause a public nuisance too, in which case the government can come in and file a case for public nuisance). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., the right to quiet enjoyment), there is hardness (e.g., the duty of care in the right to quiet enjoyment, which can be punished if violated, be it on the basis of money or injunction). And the reverse direction also holds true. Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 233 In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by the enforcement of the law of nuisance, as shown in the problems pointed out by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by the enforcement of the law of nuisance, for the protection of the right to quiet enjoyment). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors, regardless of whether this be done by way of tort law or by way of individual agreements, in regard to nuisance), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of tort law for the institutionalized order in political society—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of individual agreements for the non-institutioinalized order in the private sphere). And the reverse direction also holds true. Silence and Culture Silence, when examined from the perspective of culture, can cast an illuminating light on its possibility and desirability, and this can be shown by way of two case studies, namely, (3.5.1) silence, contemplation, and religion and (3.5.2) silence, and the rhetorical device in debate—to be addressed in what follows, respectively. Silence, Contemplation, and Religion A good case study here to understand silence from the perspective of culture has to do with silence, contemplation, and religion. Silence Love in Religion The word “contemplation” here has a different meaning when used in the context of religion to understand silence. For instance, in Christian religion, especially in the version known as “Christian mysticism,” the word “contemplation” refers to “a form of prayer distinct from vocal prayer (recitation of words) and from meditation in the strict sense (a form of mental prayer, also called methodical prayer, based on discursive reflection on various considerations).” (WK 2010bb; W. Johnston 1997; LEV 2010) In accordance to the Catechism of the Catholic Church—“[t]he Christian tradition comprises three major expressions of the life of prayer: The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 234 vocal prayer, meditation, and contemplative prayer. They have in common the recollection of the heart.” (WK 2010bb) But contemplation differs from both vocal prayer (or recitation) and meditation, in that it is, in the Christian tradition, “a silent love.” (WK 2010bb) Meditation and Contemplation The silent love in contemplation differs from “meditation” in different ways, according to different interpretations. Consider a few examples below, for illustration, as summarized in Table 3.6. Firstly, in accordance to the Catechism of the Catholic Church, “[i]n discursive meditation, mind and imagination and other faculties are actively employed in an effort to understand our relationship with God.” (WK 2010bb) But “[i]n contemplative prayer, this activity is curtailed, so that contemplation has been described as 'a gaze of faith,' 'a silent love.'” (WK 2010bb) Secondly, in accordance to Saint John of the Cross (1906), “the difference between discursive meditation and contemplation” is like this: “The difference between these two conditions of the soul is like the difference between working, and enjoyment of the fruit of our work; between receiving a gift, and profiting by it; between the toil of travelling and the rest of our journey's end.” (WK 2010bb; B. Frost 1935) Thirdly, in accordance to an Oriental Orthodox expert, Mattá al- Miskīn (2003), “[m]editation is an activity of one's spirit by reading or otherwise, while contemplation is a spontaneous activity of that spirit. In meditation, man's imaginative and thinking power exert some effort. Contemplation then follows to relieve man of all effort. Contemplation is the soul's inward vision and the heart's simple repose in God.” (WK 2010bb) But for al-Miskīn, “[t]here is no clear-cut boundary between Christian meditation and Christian contemplation, and they sometimes overlap. Meditation serves as a foundation on which the contemplative life stands, the practice by which someone begins the state of contemplation.” (WK 2010bb) Two Kinds of Contemplation With these different interpretations in mind—there are two kinds of contemplation to be understood, namely, (a) natural and (b) supernatural— Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 235 as discussed below, in that order (and summarized in Table 3.6). (WK 2010bb; A. Poulain 1908) (a) Natural Contemplation The first kind of contemplation is called “natural” (also known as “acquired”) and “[o]ver the centuries,…has been called by various names such as the Prayer of Faith, Prayer of the Heart, Prayer of Simplicity, Prayer of Simple Regard, Active Recollection, Active Quiet and Acquired Contemplation.” (WK 2010bb; T. Keating 1991) In any event, natural contemplation “has been comapred to the attitude of a mother watching over the cradle of her child: she thinks lovingly of the child without reflection and amid interruptions.” (WK 2010bb) As Saint Alphonsus Maria de Liguori argued, natural contemplation “consists in seeing at a simple glance the truths which could previously be discovered only through prolonged discourse”; so “reasoning is largely replaced by intuition,” and “affections and resolutions, though not absent, are only slightly varied and expressed in a few words.” (WK 2010bb) But there is something central in natural contemplation, “known as the prayer of simplicity or of simple gaze,” which “recurs constantly and easily (although with little or no development) amid many other thoughts, beneficial or otherwise. The prayer of simplicity often has a tendency to simplify itself even in respect to its object, leading one to think chiefly of God and of his presence, but in a confused manner.” (WK 2010bb; A. Poulain 1908) This simple devotion to God in natural contemplation is, for Adolphe Tanquerey, “a simple gaze on God and divine things proceeding from love and tending thereto” and, for Saint Francis de Sales, “a loving, simple and permanent attentiveness of the mind to divine things.” (WK 2010bb; W. Johnston 2004) Or, for St. Teresa, the prayer of simplicity “means taking time frequently to be alone with him who we know loves us” and seeking “him 'whom my soul loves.' It is Jesus, and in him, the Father. We seek him, because to desire him is always the beginning of love, and we seek him in that pure faith which causes us to be born of him and to live in him. In this inner prayer we can still meditate, but our attention is fixed on the Lord himself.” (WK 2010bb) And “[a] person is known to be called to natural contemplation because of succeeding in it with ease, and benefitting from it. This is especially so, if the person has a persistent attraction to this kind of prayer together with difficulty and distaste for discursive meditation.” (WK 2010bb) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 236 (b) Superatural Contemplation The second kind of contemplation is called “supernatural” (and also known as “infused,” “higher,” “intuitive,” “passive,” and even “extraordinary”) and refers to “a supernatural gift by which a person's mind and will become totally centered on God.” (WK 2010bb) Supernatural contemplation is therefore higher than natural contemplation, as it is “a form of mystical union with God, a union characterized by the fact that it is God, and God only, who manifests himself. Under this influence of God, which assumes the free cooperation of the human will, the intellect receives special insights into things of the spirit, and the affections are extraordinarily animated with divine love. This union that it entails may be linked with manifestations of a created object, as, for example, visions of the humanity of Christ or an angel or revelations of a future event, etc. They include miraculous bodily phenomena sometimes observed in ecstatics.” (WK 2010bb; A. Poulain 1908) Bernhard Häring once described supernatural contemplation in this beautiful way: “[I]n this mystical experience the 'divine partner in the dialogue' is in the foreground rather than the human response. In mystical prayer, the soul experiences the life in grace and from grace as a gift of divine love. It is the experience of faith in its most exalted realization.” (WK 2010bb) For Thomas Dubay (1989), supernatural contemplation is only among “those who try to live the whole Gospel wholeheartedly and who engage in an earnest prayer life”; and, for John Baptist Scaramelli, “asceticism and mysticism are two distinct paths to perfection, the former being the normal, ordinary end of the Christian life, and the latter something extraordinary and very rare.” (WK 2010bb; J. Aumann 1985) It is no wonder that, for some scholars like Jordan Aumann (1985), “this idea of the two paths was 'an innovation in spiritual theology and a departure from the traditional Catholic teaching.'” (WK 2010b) And, for Saint Teresa of Avila, there are “four degrees or stages of mystical union” in supernatural contemplation, as shown below: (Wk 2010bb) • “Incomplete Mystical Union”—is “the prayer of quiet or supernatural recollection, when the action of God is not strong enough to prevent distractions, and the imagination still retains a certain liberty” • “Full or Semi-Ecstatic Union”—is the stage “when the strength of the divine action keeps the person fully occupied but the senses continue to act, so that by making an effort, the person can cease from prayer” Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 237 • “Ecstatic Union”—is the stateg “when communications with the external world are severed or nearly so, and one can no longer at will move from that state” • “Transforming or Deifying Union”—is the “spiritual marriage (properly) of the soul with God” Thus, “[t]he first three are weak, medium, and the energetic states of the same grace,” but the last one is the final “spiritual marriage of the soul with God.” Problems with Silent Love But this idea of the higher form of supernatural contemplation (for “silent love”) is not with criticisms. Consider, for illustration, a few of them below, as summarized in Table 3.6. Firstly, one major criticism of the idea of supernatural contemplation is that it is elitist, only for a few who can make it, while the rest of humanity are not qualified. After all, Dubay (1989) himself acknowledged that supernatural contemplation is only among “those who try to live the whole Gospel wholeheartedly and who engage in an earnest prayer life”; and, for John Baptist Scaramelli, “asceticism and mysticism are two distinct paths to perfection, the former being the normal, ordinary end of the Christian life, and the latter something extraordinary and very rare.” (WK 2010bb; J. Aumann 1985) Secondly, another major criticism of the idea of supernatural contemplation is that it is not universally accepted in the Christian community. After all, the idea of supernatural contemplation is popular within “Christian mysticism,” which, as Jordan Aumann (1985) warned us, is “a departure from the traditional Catholic teaching.'” (WK 2010b) And thirdly, still another major criticism of the idea of supernatural contemplation is that its distinction between meditation and contemplation is arbitrary from the perspective of Christian mysticism, with the inherent bias (or favoritism) for contemplation over meditation. There are historical reasons for this bias for contemplation over meditation in Christian mysticism. Historically, one should remember that “[t]he non-discursive components or stages of meditative practice, which are often called 'contemplation' in Western traditions, were beneficiaries of 'a positive attitude toward contemplation [that] characterized the first fifteen centuries of the Christian era.' But 'a negative attitude has prevailed The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 238 from the sixteenth century onward,' according to Thomas Keating [1997].” (WK 2010cc) For Keating (1997), “the emergence of a negative attitude towards contemplation” had much to do with “the 17th century controversy over Quietism and an increasing tendency to distinguish between 'discursive meditation if thoughts predominated; affective prayer if the emphasis was on acts of the will; and contemplation if graces infused by God were predominant….This division of the development of prayer into compartmentalized units entirely separate from one another helped to further the….notion that contemplation was an extraordinary grace reserved to the few.'” (WK 2010cc) Thus, the idea of supernatural contemplation is no longer popular nowadays as it used to be during “the first fifteen centuries of the Christian era.” Beyond Sacredness and Secularness These criticisms against the idea of supernatural contemplation for “silent love” are not meant to totally discredit its persuasion but only show us the two opposing sides of the debate, such that the possibility and desirability of silence (from the perspective of culture with silence, contemplation, and religion as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. Furthermore, the analysis of silence, contemplation, and religion can teach us something valuable about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the formalness-informalness principle, the absoluteness-relativeness principle, the predictability- unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness-vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution-transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness-hardness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same-difference principle. For instance, in relation to the formalness-informalness principle, if there is formalness (e.g., the formal logical requirement of completeness in a system of ideas, like the discourse on contemplation), there is informalness (e.g., the non-formal existence of incompleteness in the discourse on contemplation, to the point that it cannot prove itself, because it was based on an inherent bias for contemplation over meditation, due to Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 239 some historical reasons as pointed out by Keating). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute positive view of contemplation during “the first fifteen centuries of the Christian era”), there is relativeness (e.g., what was true for contemplation to be preferred over meditation during “the first fifteen centuries of the Christian era” is not necessarily so in modern times, with “the emergence of a negative attitude towards contemplation”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictability (e.g., the predictable tendency of a believer in Christian mysticism to practice contemplation over meditation), there is unpredictability (e.g., the more difficult task to predict which particular believer will succeed in passing through which particular stages of “mystical union” with God, since only a few will ever make it, which is “something extraordinary and very rare”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g., the explanation by John of the Cross that contemplation is higher than meditation in prayer because “the difference between discursive meditation and contemplation” is “like the difference between working, and enjoyment of the fruit of our work; between receiving a gift, and profiting by it; between the toil of travelling and the rest of our journey's end”), there is inexplicability (e.g., the lack of suffiicient explanation by John of the Cross of why this favoritism of contemplation over meditation is necessarily true, since, for the critics like Keating, the biased comparison could be explained by some contingent historical reasons). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g., the precise classification, by Saint Teresa of Avila, of “mystical union” in supernatural contemplation in terms of “four degrees or stages”), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the classification, since it is not clear why there are only four degrees or stages, not five, six, seven, and so on). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple analysis of contemplation in accordance to Christian mysticism), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated analysis of contemplation by questioning its assumptions and claims, as shown in the criticisms by the critics). And the reverse direction also holds true. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 240 In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of the relationships between meditation and contemplation in accordance to Christian mysticism), there is hiddenness (e.g., the hidden bias for contemplation in the analysis of the relationships, because of the contingent historical reasons as pointed out by Keating). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of Christian believers who preferred contemplation over meditation in “the first fifteen centuries of the Christian era”), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more empty, concentration of Christian believers who prefer contemplation over meditation nowadays). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower speed of someone in the final stage of “mystical union” in contemplative prayer to get distracted), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively faster speed of someone in the first stage of “mystical union” in contemplative prayer to get distracted). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relative expansion of the influence of meditation from the 18th century until now, in the Christian tradition), there is contraction (e.g., the relative decline of the influence of contemplation from the 18th century until now, in the Christian tradition). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of contemplation in philosophy, theology, and psychology, for instance), there is praxis (e.g,., the practical application of contemplation to the field of Christian mysticism for “mystical union” with God). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional positive wisdom about contemplation over meditation in the older days), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to this conventional wisdom about contemplation, by the new idea that supernatural contemplation is higher than natural contemplation, as Aumann once pointed out that “this idea of the two paths was 'an innovation in spiritual theology and a departure from the traditional Catholic teaching'”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to use their mental faculties like imagination, reasoning, intuition, etc. in the state of nature), Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 241 there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human ability to use their mental faculties by the invention of systems of ideas like Christian mysticism for prefering contemplation over meditation). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the existence of different stages of mystical union in contemplative prayer), there is asymmetry (e.g., the first three stages are not fully in mystical union with God—but the final stage is fully in mystical union with God, in accordance to Christian mysticism). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., the reward of mystical union with God, in accordance to Christian mysticism), there is hardness (e.g., only a few will make it to the final stage of mystical union with God, in accordance to Christian mysticism). In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by contemplative prayer, as shown in the criticisms by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by contemplative prayer for spiritual enlightenment). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors, regardless of whether this be done by way of contemplative prayer or by way of discursive meditation), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of contemplative prayer for a sacred worldview based more on graces—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and behaviors by way of discursive meditation for a sacred worldview based more on thoughts). And the reverse direction also holds true. Silence, Abduction, and the Rhetorical Device in Debate Another way to evaluate the possibility and desirability of silence from the perspective of culture concerns silence, abduction, and the rhetorical device in debate. Argument from Silence, and Abduction The term “argument from silence” (also known as argumentum ex silentio in Latin) refers to “a conclusion based on silence or lack of contrary evidence.” (WK 2010dd; OED 1999) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 242 For instance, in classical studies, “it often refers to the deduction from the lack of references to a subject in the available writings of an author to the conclusion that he was ignorant of it. When used as a logical proof in pure reasoning, the argument is classed among the fallacies, but an argument from silence can be a convincing form of abductive reasoning,” which is neither deduction nor induction. (WK 2010dd; COD 2006) A deductive argument may be valid or invalid, an inductive argument may be probable or improbable, but an abductive argument may be reasonable or unreasonable. Some Textbook Examples of the Argument from Silence For illustration, hereafter is a good example, where an argument from silence may not be reasonable: (WK 2010dd) • Bobby: “I know where Mary lives.” • Billy: “Where?” • Bobby: “I'm not telling you!” • Billy: “You're just saying that because you don't know!” In this example, “Billy's conclusion may not be justified: perhaps Bobby doesn't want to tell him.” (WK 2010dd) By contrast, consider the following example, where an argument from silence may be reasonable: (WK 2010dd) • John: “Do you know any Spanish?” • Jack: “Of course. I speak it like a native.” • John: “That's good, because I need to know the Spanish phrase for 'Happy Birthday.'” • Jack: “Sorry, I don't have time for that right now. Maybe tomorrow. Bye.” In this example, “Jack continually refuses to give John the Spanish translation, either by ignoring John or by giving excuses. John then concludes, by argument from silence, that Jack does not in fact know Spanish or does not know it well. In other words, John believes that Jack's ignorance is the most plausible explanation for his silence. Use of argument from silence in this situation is reasonable given that the alternatives, that Jack either doesn't want or is afraid to translate, would be unreasonable without more information.” (WK 2010dd) Hereafter is still another example, where the argument from silence may not be reasonable: (WK 2010dd) Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 243 • John: “Do you know your wife's e-mail password?” • Jack: “Yes, I do as a matter of fact.” • John: “What is it?” • Jack: “Hey, that's none of your business.” In this example, “[w]hen John repeatedly asked for the password, Jack ignores him completely. Thus, using the argument from silence, John concludes that Jack does not actually know the password. Such an argument from silence, in contrast, may be considered unreasonable, since a password is a security feature not intended to be shared with a stranger simply because they asked. It may be reasonable, by contrast, to assume that Jack does indeed know the password but refuses to say it for legitimate security concerns.” (WK 2010dd) Scholarly Uses of the Argument from Silence The argument from silence had been applied to scholarly works. Consider, for illustration, two historical examples, one where the argument from silence may be reasonable but the other where it may not. In regard to a historical example where the argument from silence may be reasonable, it is known that “the editors of Yerushalmi and Bavli” did not mention each other, so “most scholars believe these documents were written independently. Louis Jacobs writes, 'If the editors of either had had access to an actual text of the other, it is inconceivable that they would not have mentioned this. Here the argument from silence is very convincing.'” (WK 2010dd; CC 1999) And in regard to a historical example where the argument from silence may not be reasonable, it is known that “[i]n the Nova/Horizon episode 'The Case of the Bermuda Triangle,' David Kusche pointed out that the argument from silence has been used to create an improper shifting of the burden of proof in many Bermuda Triangle stories and theories.” (WK 2010dd) Here is how Kusche put it, “Say I claim that a parrot has been kidnapped to teach aliens human language and I challenge you to prove that is not true. You can even use Einstein's Theory of Relativity if you like. There is simply no way to prove such a claim untrue. The burden of proof should be on the people who make these statements, to show where they got their information from, to see if their conclusions and interpretations are valid, and if they have left anything out.” (WK 2010dd) The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 244 Argument from Silence in Some Legal Traditions In some legal traditions (like the German), “juries are explicitly instructed not to infer anything because of an accused person's silence; this is known as the right to silence. Thus, the jury may not infer anything from the accused's failure to testify. This in effect bars the use of argument from silence.” (WK 2010dd) However, “statements volunteered by the accused may normally be considered, and in such cases the argument from silence may apply in a limited form. If the accused chooses to testify, the right to silence is forfeited as regards that proceeding. Witnesses also normally have a right to silence as regards any question that is factually incriminating, but that right only bars the jury from making inferences about the witness's conduct. The range of inferences available about the defendant's conduct will vary.” (WK 2010dd) In addition, “[s]ome versions of the Hearsay Rule use a form of argument by silence in that if a party fails to respond to a statement that would normally provoke a denial, this statement is considered as having been adopted by that party and can generally be used against him or her at trial. The reasoning behind this is that if the party had disagreed with the statement, he or she would have objected.” (WK 2010dd) Problems with the Argument from Silence But there are some problems with the argument from silence. Consider, for illustration, a few of them below. Firstly, one major problem with the argument from silence is that it does not tell us whether or not a conclusion is true or false but only that it may be reasonable or unreasonable—as already illustrated in the textbook examples and the historical examples. Secondly, another major problem with the argument from silence is that its application varies from one legal tradition to another and from one context to another—as already shown in the example about the German legal system, where the argument from silence is allowed only selectively. And thirdly, still another major problem with the argument from silence is that, “in pure reasoning, the argument is classed among the fallacies.” (WK 2010dd) So, what is regarded as “reasonable” in abduction is treated as “fallacious” in pure reasoning instead. A Bigger Picture Yet, these criticisms against the argument from silence do not imply to dismiss its usefulness but only show us the two opposing sides of the Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 245 debate, such that the possibility and desirability of silence (from the perspective of culture with silence, abduction, and the argument from silence as a case study here) are not to the extent that the respective defenders on both sides would like us to believe. Furthermore, the analysis of silence, abduction, and the argument from silence can reveal something important about the ontological principles in existential dialectics, and good examples include the absoluteness-relativeness principle, the predictability-unpredictability principle, the explicability-inexplicability principle, the preciseness- vagueness principle, the simpleness-complicatedness principle, the openness-hiddenness principle, the denseness-emptiness principle, the slowness-quickness principle, the expansion-contraction principle, the theory-praxis principle, the convention-novelty principle, the evolution- transformation principle, the symmetry-asymmetry principle, the softness- hardness principle, the regression-progression principle, and the same- difference principle. For instance, in relation to the absoluteness-relativeness principle, if there is absoluteness (e.g., the absolute concern with reasonableness in abduction), there is relativeness (e.g., what is regarded as “reasonable” in abduction is treated insteead as “fallacious” in pure reasoning). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the predictability-unpredictability principle, if there is predictabiltiy (e.g., the predictable tendency of abduction to have a conclusion which is reasonable or unreasonable), there is unpredictability (.e.g, the more difficult task to predict beforehand which particular conversation will end up being abductive in nature, not deductive nor inductive, and which particular one will be reasonable or unreasonable). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the explicability-inexplicability principle, if there is explicability (e.g, the explanation by those using abductive reasoning that the conclusion may not reasonable under certain conditions, as shown in the textbook and historical examples), there is inexplicability (.e.g, the lack of convincing explanation, by those in abduction, of why being reasonable in abduction cannot be fallacious at all, at least for the critics in pure reasoning). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the preciseness-vagueness principle, if there is preciseness (e.g,. the precise classification of reasoning in terms of three kinds, namely, deduction, induction, and abduction), there is vagueness (e.g., the vagueness in the classification of reasoning in terms of three kinds, since it is not clear why the traditional classification of only two types, namely, deduction and induction, is not necessarily better, or why The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 246 the kinds of reasoning cannot be four, five, and so on). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the simpleness-complicatedness principle, if there is simpleness (e.g., the relatively simple analysis of abduction by its advocates), there is complicatedness (e.g., the relatively more complicated analysis of abduction by questioning its assumptions and claims, as shown in the criticisms by the critics). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the openness-hiddenness principle, if there is openness (e.g., the open exploration of the three kinds of reasoning), there is hiddenness (e.g., the hidden bias in each kind of reasoning, because each is concerned with its own version of legitimacy in logic, be it about validity, probability, or reasonableness). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the denseness-emptiness principle, if there is denseness (e.g., the relatively denser concentration of those in pure reasoning to regard abductive reasoning as “fallacious”), there is emptiness (e.g., the relatively less dense, or more empty, concentration of those in abduction to regard abductive reasoning as “fallacious”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the slowness-quickness principle, if there is slowness (e.g., the relatively slower readiness of a specialist in abduction to make a conclusion which is valid or invalid), there is quickness (e.g., the relatively quicker readiness of a specialist in abduction to make a conclusion which is reasonable or unreasonable). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the expansion-contraction principle, if there is expansion (e.g., the relatively more developed ability of an expert in abduction to analyze the reasonableness of an argument), there is contraction (e.g., the relatively less developed ability of an expert in abduction to analyze the validity or probability of an argument). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the theory-praxis principle, if there is theory (e.g., the theoretical construction of abduction in logic), there is praxis (e.g., the practical application of abduction to the field of legal systems in Germany, especially in relation to “statements volunteered by the accused”). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the convention-novelty principle, if there is convention (e.g., the conventional wisdom about reasoning in terms of deduction and induction), there is novelty (e.g., the alternative novel challenge to the conventional wisdom about reasoning, by the creation of abduction as the third kind of reasoning). And the reverse direction also holds true. Chapter 3: Silence and Its Duality 247 In relation to the evolution-transformation principle, if there is evolution (e.g., the natural evolution of humans to reason, at least in a primitive way, in the state of nature), there is transformation (e.g., the technical transformation of human ability to reason by the invention of some formal systems of reasoning, like deduction, induction, and abduction). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the symmetry-asymmetry principle, if there is symmetry (e.g., the existence of three different kinds of reasoning), there is asymmetry (e.g., deduction focuses on the validity of an argument, induction focuses on the probability of an argument, and abduction focuses on the reasonableness of an argument). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the softness-hardness principle, if there is softness (e.g., the praise of someone’s argument as reasonable), there is hardness (e.g., the criticism of someone’s argument as unreasonable). And the reverse direction also holds true. In relation to the regression-progression principle, if there is regression (e.g., the regression made by abduction, as shown in the criticisms by the critics), there is progression (e.g., the progress made by abduction for a different kind of argument based on reasonableness). And the reverse direction also holds true. And in relation to the same-difference principle, if there is similarity in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values, regardless of whether this be done by way of pure reasoning or by way of abductive reasoning), there is difference in outcome (e.g., the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of pure reasoning for a relatively strict form of rationality—but the contribution to the molding and regulation of beliefs and values by way of abductive reasoning for a relatively speculative form of rationality). And the reverse direction also holds true. The Turmoil of Silence This comprehensive analysis of the possibility and desirability of silence, from the perspectives of the mind, nature, society, and culture, has shown us the different ways in which silence is both possible and desirable, but not to the extent that the spokespersons from each side would like us to believe. Silence has its turmoil as the dark side, just as it has its serenity as the bright side—so to speak. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 248 But this is only one part of a larger story, since there is the other side of the story, which concerns sound, the opposite of silence—which, however, was already dealt with in Chapter Two. These dual analyses are important enough, because those on the side of sound often downgrades silence merely as the opposite of sound without really appreciating it from the vantage point of silence too. With this completion of the dual analyses here, what then can be concluded at the end of this intellectual journey?
