See book for citations. • PART FOUR • _____________________________________ Conclusion CHAPTER 4 CO�CLUSIO�—THE FUTURE OF ACOUSTICS _____________________________________ I believe that the use of noise to make music will continue and increase until we reach a music produced through the aid of electrical instruments which will make available for musical purposes any and all sounds that can be heard. —John Cage (WK 2010ee) Beyond Sound and Silence The analyses of sound (in Chapter Two) and silence (in Chapter Three) are to reveal the extent of their possibility and desirability in acoustics. These analyses should not be underestimated, in light of the opposing views on the nature of sound and silence (as already described in Sec. 1.1 and the rest of the book). Contrary to the different opposing views (as introduced in this book), sound and silence are neither possible nor desirable to the extent that their respective ideologues would like us to believe. Now, one should not misconstrue this critique of the conventional wisdom about the nature of sound and silence in acoustics as a suggestion that it is a worthless field of study, or that some fields of study (related to acoustics) like music, mathematical acoustics, psychoacoustics, architectural acoustics, and so on are to be ignored. Obviously, neither of these extreme views is reasonable either. Instead, this book provides an alternative (better) way to understand the future of acoustics, especially in the dialectic context of sound and silence—while learning from different approaches in the literature but The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 260 without favoring any one of them (nor integrating them, since they are not necessarily compatible with each other). In other words, this book offers a new theory (that is, the multilateral theory of acoustics) to go beyond the existing approaches in the literature on acoustics in an original way. My multilateral theory of acoustics has four major distinct features. Firstly, my theory makes good use of all theoretical approaches in the literature on sound and silence, be they about the mental argument, the natural argument, the societal argument, or the cultural argument— especially from the most comprehensive combined perspectives of the mind, nature, society, and culture (as will be clear in Chapter Two and Chapter Three). Secondly, just like many other theories of mine in my previous books, my theory here does not heavily favor any specific theory over others in the literature, nor trying to integrate them (as they are not necessarily compatible with each other). For this reason, the word “multilateral” in the title of the theory is suggestive. Thirdly, my theory treats the issue of acoustics in the distinctive dialectic context of sound and silence, such that one is not to be reduced as part of the analysis of the other. And fourthly, it contains seventeen major theses, namely, (a) the first thesis: the absoluteness-relativeness principle, (b) the second thesis: the predictability-unpredictability principle, (c) the third thesis: the explicability-inexplicability principle, (d) the fourth thesis: the preciseness-vagueness principle, (e) the fifth thesis: the simpleness- complicatedness principle, (f) the sixth thesis: the openness-hiddenness principle, (g) the seventh thesis: the denseness-emptiness principle, (h) the eighth thesis: the slowness-quickness principle, (i) the nineth thesis: the expansion-contraction principle, (j) the tenth thesis: the theory-praxis principle, (k) the eleventh thesis: the convention-novelty principle, (l) the twelveth thesis: the evolution-transformation principle, (m) the thirteenth thesis: the symmetry-asymmetry principle, (n) the fourteenth thesis: the softness-hardness principle, (o) the fifteenth thesis: the regression- progression principle, (p) the sixteenth thesis: the sameness-difference principle, and (q) the seventeenth thesis: the post-human creativeness—to be elaborated in the rest of the book, with a summary in the concluding chapter. Of course, as this is something that I often emphasized in my previous books, other principles (besides the 16 as cited above) are also relevant, but these 16 are the most relevant in the current case study (in terms of the number of citations of each principle in the book). Chapter 4: Conclusion—The Future of Acoustics 261 Even then, in some cases, the difference between any two given principles, for instance, in terms of the number of citations in a book, is rather small, so the reason in those cases is more aesthetic (than otherwise), because it looks nicer to list only 16 theses for 16 principles (than 22 theses for all of the 22 principles) in the Table of Contents. This is true, even if different studies of the same kind can yield different views about the degree of relevance for each principle, depending on the specific nature of a research in question, needless to say. So, if a different author analyzes the same subject matter in a different way, the relevance of the principles will be different. With this clarification in mind—if successful, this seminal project is to fundamentally change the way that we think about acoustics, from the combined perspectives of the mind, nature, society, and culture, with enormous implications for the human future and what I originally called its “post-human” fate. In the Category of Method Firstly, in regard to the formalness-informalness principle (on the formal requirements of logical systems), if there is formalness (e.g., the formal logical requirement of completeness in scientific work, like the research on animals using infrasound to predict disaster, in Sec. 3.3.1; and the formal logical requirement of completeness in a system of ideas, like the discourse on contemplation, in Sec. 3.5.1), there is informalenss too (e.g., the non-formal existence of incompleteness in the research on animals using infrasound to predict disaster, because “[i]t is not known for sure if this is the exact reason, as some have suggested that it was the influence of electromagnetic waves, and not of infrasonic waves, that prompted these animals to flee,” in Sec. 3.3.1; and the non-formal existence of incompleteness in the discourse on contemplation, to the point that it cannot prove itself, because it was based on an inherent bias for contemplation over meditation, due to some historical reasons as pointed out by Keating, in Sec. 3.5.1). In the Category of Agency Firstly, in regard to the seriousness-playfulness principle (on the extent of seriousness), if there is seriousness (e.g., an extrovert can be serious in political public demonstrations, in Sec. 2.2.2; the serious business of a male whale to make sounds to a female whale for reproduction, in Sec. 2.3.1; the serious business of social functions in small talk, in Sec. 2.4.2; the serious nature of chaotic music for a different musical sensibility, in Sec .2.5.1; and the serious business by those in noise music to create a new kind of music, in Sec. 2.5.2), there is playfulness (e.g., an extrovert can enjoy himself by having fun in loud parties, like in political public demonstrations, in Sec. 2.2.2; the playful nature of a male whale to make sounds to a female whale for seduction, in Sec. 2.3.1; the playful nature of small talk, when men engage in “playful insults,” in Sec. 2.4.2; the playful nature of chaotic music when it plays with chance in the composition, in Sec. 2.5.1; and the playful nature by those in noise music to play with different techniques and instruments in the process of creating new music, in Sec. 2.5.2). And the reverse direction also holds true. 1st Thesis: The Absoluteness-Relativeness Principle The first thesis refers to the absoluteness-relativeness principle (on the multiplicity of things) in the category of “method” in existential dialectics, The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 264 which was first proposed in FPHK, in that there is the multiplicity of things in reality, be they about entities, qualities (or properties), and relationships. If there is something absolute, there is likewise something relative. And there is no absoluteness without relativeness—and vice versa. Both absoluteness and relativeness here are also relevant to different modalities often cited in the literature on ontology, such as possibility (e.g., something “can” happen) and its opposite (e.g., impossibility), probability (e.g., something “will” happen) and its opposite (e.g., improbability), and necessity (e.g., something “should” happen) and its opposite (e.g., contingency). There is no predictability without unpredictability—and vice versa. There are events which are predictable, just as there are those which are not. Or what is regarded as unpredictable at one point in time may turn out to be predictable later, and, conversely, what is deemed as predictable may turn out to not be so predictable. Even in predictability, outcomes are subject to uncertainty, the degree of which varies from case to case. There is no explicability without inexplicability— and vice versa. This principle tells us the dual nature of the research dilemma, in that, if reality can be explained in some ways, it also has its other ways which are not quite explainable, at a given point in time. The Future of Post-Human Acoustics 272 4th Thesis: The Preciseness-Vagueness Principle The fourth thesis is called the preciseness-vagueness principle (on the refinement of things) in the category of “structure” in existential dialectics (which was first out worked out in FIA), in that both preciseness and vagueness are important, not that one is better than the other, but that both are used, in different degrees of preference, in accordance to the contextual application from the perspectives of nature, the mind, culture, and society. There is no preciseness without vagueness—and vice versa. Firstly, the word “post-human” here should not be confused with another term which looks similar but has a totally different meaning in the literature of postmodernism, namely, “post-humanism”—which constitutes a critique of “humanism” as tradionally understood (especially, though not exclusively, in relation to the idea of progress in science and reason in the Enlightenment project). My critique of “transhumanism” was more extensively elabroated in Sec. 2.4.1 of BEPE. Thirdly, the post-human creativeness in acoustics will learn from the multilateral theory of acoustics in relation to the non-privilege of any specific theory over others in the literature and the non-integration of them all (as they are not necessarily compatible with each other). Five Great Future Transformations of Acoustics The five great future transformations of acoustics can be explained hereafter, with the caveat, however, that the classification in terms of five is solely aesthetic and utilitarian (illustrative), as there is no objective basis that it must be classified in term of five. The First Great Future Transformation of Acoustics The first great future transformation of acoustics in the post-human era concerns what I originally call new sound detection. This new sound detection allows future advanced humans and later their successors, namely, the post-humans, the ability to hear and detect sound in a way that current humans cannot. There are already some indications that the future of acoustics is moving toward this direciton. Consider, for illustration, a few examples below. Firstly, submarine undercover navigation systems and anti-submarine warfare detection systems nowadays (as already discussed in Sec. 2.4.1) point to the need for more sophisticated sound detection ability. Chapter 4: Conclusion—The Future of Acoustics 303 Secondly, the use of seismographs to detect seismic waves for earthquake prediction nowadays (as already discussed in Sec. 2.4.2) points to another need for more sophisticated sound detection ability. Thirdly, the search for what I originally called “the potential of unfolding unconsciousness” (as already discussed in my book titled The Future of Post-Human U nconsciousess in 2008), especially in relation to “clair-audience” (in hearing), “clair-sentience” (in feeling), and “clair- cognizance” (in knowing), for instance, points to one additional need for more sophisticated sound detection ability. All these are just some illustrative (relatively primitive) examples, of course, but the important point to remember here is that the quest for more sophisticated sound detection will further transform acoustics at the more advanced level in the post-human future that the human world has never known. Enormous Implications These future great transformations of sound and silence in acoustics have enormous implications for some of the profound questions which have intrigued some of the finest minds in human history—Is there “clair- audience” (in hearing) for intelligent life to hear in an unusual way never possible before? Can meditation and contemplation in a state of silence bring the mind of intelligent life to be in union with the cosmos (or something of that nature)? And….? Questions like this will yield new answers in post-human acoustics in the current dialectic context of (a) treating both sound and silence and (b) going beyond sound and silence—such that their possibility and desirability are not to the extent that the respective defenders would like us to believe. In fact, some of my other books titled The Future of Post-Human Religion (2010), Beyond Cosmology to Post-Cosmology (2010), and The Future of Post-Human Unconsciousness (2008) had already dealt with issues of this nature, though from different vantage points. This clarification aside—an important point to remember here is that the five great future transformations of sound and silence in acoustics will bring neither utopia nor dystopia—as this is something that I have warned time and again in all of my previous books. After all, it is not up to humans to judge whether or not, or to what extent, the post-human future of acoustics will be for better and for worse, because it will be decided by the values and beliefs of future post-humans in a way that the entire history of our human world hitherto existing has never encountered. But it is already a giant step for us to take if we can acknowledge this bold vision of the five future transformation of acoustics, so as to contribute to the better understanding of the future of acoustics and its post-human fate. Five Theses on Post-Civilization ____________________________________________________________ • Post-civilization no longer treats civilization as good and barbarity as evil (relatively speaking), nor does it nostalgically regard barbarity as good and civilization as evil (relatively speaking again). Civilization is as evil and good as barbarity. • Post-civilization also no longer accepts the dichotomy between civilization and barbarity. Civilization cannot exist without barbarity. It is no longer necessary to preserve civilization, any more than it is imperative to destroy barbarity. To go beyond civilization and barbarity is to acknowledge the co-existence of both, although the degree of scaling one over the over varies from case to case—but is not to be extreme in largely favoring one over the other, on average (subject to the constraints of existential dialectics). • Post-civilization is thus subject to the constraints of existential dialectics. There is no freedom without unfreedom, and no equality without inequality, for instance. There will be no utopia; even should there be one, there would be dystopia embedded within it. • Post-civilization will eventually replace civilization (as a form of life settlement), to be dominated by post-capitalist and post-democratic lifeforms here on earth and in deep space (besides other alien lifeforms that we have never known), unto the post-human age in multiverses.
